# Canonical Ubuntu 22.04 LTS STIG: Explained

*Canonical Ubuntu 22.04 LTS Security Technical Implementation Guide*, V2R10, benchmark date 30 Sep 2026. 191 rules. Generated by STIG Explorer 1.0.0 on 2026-11-15 21:34 UTC.



## How to read this document

Every rule is explained at three levels. Read the one that fits you, or all three:

- **Level 3: General Audience.** Plain language and an everyday analogy, for readers with little security or IT background.
- **Level 2: System Administrator.** The exact settings changed, where they live, how to check and fix them, and the operational impact.
- **Level 1: Cyber Security Professional.** DISA's risk rationale, threat context and MITRE ATT&CK techniques, and the CCI to NIST SP 800-53 Rev 3 / Rev 4 / Rev 5 control mapping.

Check and fix procedures, vulnerability discussions and CCI definitions are quoted from DISA's published STIG and CCI List. Topic explanations, threat context and plain-language summaries are written by STIG Explorer and should be read as guidance, not as authoritative DISA text. **The DISA STIG is always the authoritative source for compliance.**

### V-278951 · UBTU-22-211000 · CAT I: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS must be a vendor-supported release.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-278951r1268251_rule` |
| Severity | CAT I (high) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Patching & Supported Software |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be a vendor-supported release.

**Why it matters:** Software makers regularly release fixes for security holes they discover. This rule requires installing those fixes and only running versions that are still supported. It's like getting the recall repair on your car: skip it, and the known problem stays there for anyone to take advantage of.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep DISTRIB_DESCRIPTION /etc/lsb-release
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
pro status
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** Patch from approved repositories with 'apt-get update && apt-get upgrade' (or 'unattended-upgrades' for automatic security updates). Review pending updates with 'apt list --upgradable'. Check the release with 'lsb_release -a' against Canonical's support lifecycle; an Ubuntu Pro subscription extends security maintenance (ESM).

**Operational impact:** Patching requires maintenance windows and sometimes reboots. Test critical applications against updates in a staging environment, but don't let testing stretch beyond IAVM deadlines.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the version of Ubuntu 22.04 LTS is vendor supported with the following command:

$ grep DISTRIB_DESCRIPTION /etc/lsb-release
DISTRIB_DESCRIPTION="Ubuntu 22.04.1 LTS"

Check the subscription status of the system with the following command:
$ pro status

If the installed version of Ubuntu 22.04 LTS is not supported, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Upgrade to a supported version of Ubuntu 22.04 LTS.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** An operating system release is considered "supported" if the vendor continues to provide security patches for the product. With an unsupported release, it will not be possible to resolve security issues discovered in the system software.

The support status of the OS depends on its subscription status.

End of life dates for Ubuntu 22.04 releases are as follows:
Standard Support: April 2027
Extended Security Maintenance (ESM): April 2032

ESM is available via an Ubuntu Pro subscription.

**Threat & control context:** Known, unpatched vulnerabilities remain the most common initial-access and privilege-escalation vector. Running an unsupported release means new vulnerabilities will never be fixed. SI-2 (flaw remediation) and SA-22 (unsupported system components) require timely patching per organizational timelines (IAVM compliance in DoD) and replacement of end-of-life components. Unsupported OS findings are CAT I because they can't be mitigated by configuration alone.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application; T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

### V-260469 · UBTU-22-211015 · CAT I: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS must disable the x86 Ctrl-Alt-Delete key sequence.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-260469r1268251_rule` |
| Severity | CAT I (high) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Boot Process & Console Security |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Service (systemd) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must disable the x86 Ctrl-Alt-Delete key sequence.

**Why it matters:** While a computer is starting up, before the normal sign-in screen appears, there are special "maintenance doors" that can skip the usual security. This rule puts locks on those doors and makes sure the computer only starts with trusted software, like making sure nobody can hot-wire a car by tampering with it before the key is turned.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Service | systemd | ctrl-alt-del.target | disable |
| Service | systemd | ctrl-alt-del.target | mask |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
systemctl status ctrl-alt-del.target
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
systemctl is-enabled ctrl-alt-del.target; systemctl is-active ctrl-alt-del.target
```

Expected: Expect disabled / inactive.

**How it works:** Create a GRUB superuser password hash with 'grub-mkpasswd-pbkdf2' and add 'set superusers="<name>"' and 'password_pbkdf2 <name> <hash>' to /etc/grub.d/40_custom (or 00_header), then run 'update-grub'. Kernel parameters go in GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX in /etc/default/grub, followed by 'update-grub'. Disable Ctrl-Alt-Delete with 'systemctl mask ctrl-alt-del.target' and 'systemctl daemon-reload'.

**Operational impact:** Store the boot-loader password in the system's credential vault, because you'll need it for kernel-parameter troubleshooting. Converting Legacy BIOS installs to UEFI generally requires MBR2GPT or a rebuild.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify Ubuntu 22.04 LTS is not configured to reboot the system when Ctrl-Alt-Delete is pressed by using the following command:

     $ systemctl status ctrl-alt-del.target
     ctrl-alt-del.target
          Loaded: masked (Reason: Unit ctrl-alt-del.target is masked.)
          Active: inactive (dead)

If the "ctrl-alt-del.target" is not masked, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure Ubuntu 22.04 LTS to disable the Ctrl-Alt-Delete sequence for the command line by using the following commands:

     $ sudo systemctl disable ctrl-alt-del.target

     $ sudo systemctl mask ctrl-alt-del.target

Reload the daemon to take effect:

     $ sudo systemctl daemon-reload
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** A locally logged-on user who presses Ctrl-Alt-Delete, when at the console, can reboot the system. If accidentally pressed, as could happen in the case of a mixed OS environment, this can create the risk of short-term loss of availability of systems due to unintentional reboot.

**Threat & control context:** Anyone with console or hypervisor access can interrupt the boot process to edit kernel parameters (e.g. 'init=/bin/bash'), boot into single-user or rescue mode, or load an untrusted boot loader, bypassing all OS authentication. A boot-loader password, authenticated rescue modes and UEFI Secure Boot close this path (AC-3, CM-6, SI-7(9) boot process integrity). Disabling Ctrl-Alt-Del and similar console actions prevents accidental or malicious reboots (availability).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1542 Pre-OS Boot; T1542.003 Pre-OS Boot: Bootkit; T1529 System Shutdown/Reboot

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

### V-260470 · UBTU-22-212010 · CAT I: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS, when booted, must require authentication upon booting into single-user and maintenance modes.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-260470r1268226_rule` |
| Severity | CAT I (high) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000080-GPOS-00048 |
| Topic | Boot Process & Console Security |
| CCI | CCI-000213 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-3 |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer's , when booted, must require authentication upon booting into single-user and maintenance modes.

**Why it matters:** While a computer is starting up, before the normal sign-in screen appears, there are special "maintenance doors" that can skip the usual security. This rule puts locks on those doors and makes sure the computer only starts with trusted software, like making sure nobody can hot-wire a car by tampering with it before the key is turned.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

**Key terms:**
- *root*: The all-powerful administrator account on Linux.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep -i password /boot/grub/grub.cfg
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** Create a GRUB superuser password hash with 'grub-mkpasswd-pbkdf2' and add 'set superusers="<name>"' and 'password_pbkdf2 <name> <hash>' to /etc/grub.d/40_custom (or 00_header), then run 'update-grub'. Kernel parameters go in GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX in /etc/default/grub, followed by 'update-grub'. Disable Ctrl-Alt-Delete with 'systemctl mask ctrl-alt-del.target' and 'systemctl daemon-reload'.

**Operational impact:** Store the boot-loader password in the system's credential vault, because you'll need it for kernel-parameter troubleshooting. Converting Legacy BIOS installs to UEFI generally requires MBR2GPT or a rebuild.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify Ubuntu 22.04 LTS requires a password for authentication upon booting into single-user and maintenance modes by using the following command:

     $ sudo grep -i password /boot/grub/grub.cfg

     password_pbkdf2 root grub.pbkdf2.sha512.10000.03255F190F0E2F7B4F0D1C3216012309162F022A7A636771

If the root password entry does not begin with "password_pbkdf2", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure Ubuntu 22.04 LTS to require a password for authentication upon booting into single-user and maintenance modes.

Generate an encrypted (grub) password for root by using the following command:

     $ grub-mkpasswd-pbkdf2
     Enter Password:
     Reenter Password:
     PBKDF2 hash of your password is grub.pbkdf2.sha512.10000.03255F190F0E2F7B4F0D1C3216012309162F022A7A636771

Using the hash from the output, modify the "/etc/grub.d/40_custom" file by using the following command to add a boot password:

     $ sudo sed -i '$i set superusers=\"root\"\npassword_pbkdf2 root <hash>' /etc/grub.d/40_custom

where <hash> is the hash generated by grub-mkpasswd-pbkdf2 command.

Generate an updated "grub.conf" file with the new password by using the following command:

     $ sudo update-grub
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** To mitigate the risk of unauthorized access to sensitive information by entities that have been issued certificates by DoW-approved PKIs, all DoW systems (e.g., web servers and web portals) must be properly configured to incorporate access control methods that do not rely solely on the possession of a certificate for access.

Successful authentication must not automatically give an entity access to an asset or security boundary. Authorization procedures and controls must be implemented to ensure each authenticated entity also has a validated and current authorization. Authorization is the process of determining whether an entity, once authenticated, is permitted to access a specific asset. Information systems use access control policies and enforcement mechanisms to implement this requirement.

Access control policies include identity-based policies, role-based policies, and attribute-based policies. Access enforcement mechanisms include access control lists, access control matrices, and cryptography. These policies and mechanisms must be employed by the application to control access between users (or processes acting on behalf of users) and objects (e.g., devices, files, records, processes, programs, and domains) in the information system.

**Threat & control context:** Anyone with console or hypervisor access can interrupt the boot process to edit kernel parameters (e.g. 'init=/bin/bash'), boot into single-user or rescue mode, or load an untrusted boot loader, bypassing all OS authentication. A boot-loader password, authenticated rescue modes and UEFI Secure Boot close this path (AC-3, CM-6, SI-7(9) boot process integrity). Disabling Ctrl-Alt-Del and similar console actions prevents accidental or malicious reboots (availability).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1542 Pre-OS Boot; T1542.003 Pre-OS Boot: Bootkit; T1529 System Shutdown/Reboot

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000213**: Enforce approved authorizations for logical access to information and system resources in accordance with applicable access control policies.  
  Rev 5: AC-3 · Rev 4: AC-3 · Rev 3: AC-3

### V-260471 · UBTU-22-212015 · CAT II: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS must initiate session audits at system startup.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-260471r1155214_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000254-GPOS-00095 |
| Topic | Security Event Auditing |
| CCI | CCI-001464 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-14 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-14 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-14 (1) |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must initiate session audits at system startup.

**Why it matters:** This tells the computer to write down important security events in its diary, such as who logged in, who tried and failed, and who changed a setting or used admin powers. If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.
- *Boot loader (GRUB)*: The small program that starts the operating system when the computer powers on.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/default/grub | GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT | "audit=1" |
| Config | /etc/default/grub | GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX | "audit=1" |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep -ir GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX /etc/default/grub
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep "^\s*linux" /boot/grub/grub.cfg
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo grep -rsi '^[[:space:]]*GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT\b' /etc/default/grub
```

Expected: GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT "audit=1"

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo grep -rsi '^[[:space:]]*GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX\b' /etc/default/grub
```

Expected: GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX "audit=1"

**How it works:** On Ubuntu, auditd rules are placed in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and compiled into /etc/audit/audit.rules by 'augenrules --load'. Syscall rules use '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S <syscall>'. Command rules use '-F path=<binary> -F perm=x -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k <key>'. Watches use '-w <path> -p wa -k <key>'. Supply both b32 and b64 rules where the STIG shows them. Verify the loaded rules with 'auditctl -l' and search events with 'ausearch -k <key>'.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify that Ubuntu 22.04 LTS enables auditing at system startup in GRUB.

Check the main GRUB defaults to ensure auditing is enabled:
$ sudo grep -ir GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX /etc/default/grub
/etc/default/grub:GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT="audit=1"
/etc/default/grub:GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX="audit=1"

If any Linux lines do not contain "audit=1", this is a finding.

Check the generated GRUB configuration to ensure the setting is propagated to the bootloader:
$ sudo grep "^\s*linux" /boot/grub/grub.cfg
linux   /vmlinuz-6.8.0-31-generic root=UUID=c92a542f-aee4-4af9-94b2-203624ccb8e3 ro audit=1 quiet splash $vt_handoff
linux   /vmlinuz-6.8.0-31-generic root=UUID=c92a542f-aee4-4af9-94b2-203624ccb8e3 ro recovery nomodeset dis_ucode_ldr audit=1

If any Linux lines do not contain "audit=1", this is a finding.

Note: Output details may vary by system.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure Ubuntu 22.04 LTS to produce audit records at system startup.

Edit the "/etc/default/grub" file and add "audit=1" to the "GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX" option and to the "GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT" option.

GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT="audit=1"
GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX="audit=1"

To update the grub config file, run:

$ sudo update-grub
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** If auditing is enabled late in the startup process, the actions of some startup processes may not be audited. Some audit systems also maintain state information only available if auditing is enabled before a given process is created.

**Threat & control context:** Event auditing provides the detection and forensic record for nearly every other control. The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001464**: Initiates session audits automatically at system start-up.  
  Rev 5: AU-14 (1) · Rev 4: AU-14 (1) · Rev 3: AU-14 (1)

### V-260472 · UBTU-22-213010 · CAT III: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS must restrict access to the kernel message buffer.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-260472r1268233_rule` |
| Severity | CAT III (low) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000138-GPOS-00069 |
| Topic | Kernel & Memory Exploit Mitigations |
| CCI | CCI-001090 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-4 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-4 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SC-4 |
| Implemented via | Kernel parameter (sysctl) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must restrict access to the kernel message buffer.

**Why it matters:** Hackers often break in by tricking a program into running their own instructions. These settings turn on built-in defenses that shuffle where things sit in memory and refuse to run code from places it shouldn't come from. It's like a bank regularly moving the vault around and refusing to accept instructions written on deposit slips.

**How important is it?** Low priority (CAT III): This setting adds an extra layer of protection. A gap here on its own is less likely to cause harm, but it weakens the overall defenses.

**Key terms:**
- *Kernel parameter*: A low-level switch that changes how the core of the operating system behaves.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| sysctl | /etc/sysctl.conf | kernel.dmesg_restrict | 1 |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
sysctl kernel.dmesg_restrict
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep -ir kernel.dmesg_restrict /run/sysctl.d/* /etc/sysctl.d/* /usr/local/lib/sysctl.d/* /usr/lib/sysctl.d/* /lib/sysctl.d/* /etc/sysctl.conf 2> /dev/null
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo grep -rs '^[[:space:]]*kernel.dmesg_restrict' /etc/sysctl.conf /etc/sysctl.d/ /run/sysctl.d/ /usr/local/lib/sysctl.d/ /usr/lib/sysctl.d/ /lib/sysctl.d/
```

Expected: Every match must set 1. Conflicting values in other files are a finding.

**How it works:** Set kernel tunables in /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf and apply them with 'sysctl --system'. Boot parameters are added to GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX in /etc/default/grub, followed by 'update-grub' and a reboot. Disable core dumps through /etc/security/limits.conf ('* hard core 0') and /etc/systemd/coredump.conf.

**Operational impact:** Restricting ptrace and dmesg affects debuggers (gdb, strace) for non-root users. Disabling core dumps removes crash diagnostics. HVCI can block older or unsigned drivers, so check driver compatibility first. Most sysctl changes are immediate, while boot parameters require a reboot.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify Ubuntu 22.04 LTS is configured to restrict access to the kernel message buffer by using the following command:

     $ sysctl kernel.dmesg_restrict
     kernel.dmesg_restrict = 1

If "kernel.dmesg_restrict" is not set to "1" or is missing, this is a finding.

Verify that there are no configurations that enable the kernel dmesg function:

     $ sudo grep -ir kernel.dmesg_restrict /run/sysctl.d/* /etc/sysctl.d/* /usr/local/lib/sysctl.d/* /usr/lib/sysctl.d/* /lib/sysctl.d/* /etc/sysctl.conf 2> /dev/null
     /etc/sysctl.d/10-kernel-hardening.conf:kernel.dmesg_restrict = 1

If "kernel.dmesg_restrict" is not set to "1", is commented out, is missing, or conflicting results are returned, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure Ubuntu 22.04 LTS to restrict access to the kernel message buffer.

Add or modify the following line in the "/etc/sysctl.conf" file:

kernel.dmesg_restrict = 1

Remove any configurations that conflict with the above from the following locations:

/run/sysctl.d/
/etc/sysctl.d/
/usr/local/lib/sysctl.d/
/usr/lib/sysctl.d/
/lib/sysctl.d/
/etc/sysctl.conf

Reload settings from all system configuration files by using the following command:

     $ sudo sysctl --system
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Restricting access to the kernel message buffer limits access only to root. This prevents attackers from gaining additional system information as a nonprivileged user.

**Threat & control context:** These mitigations don't remove vulnerabilities. They raise the cost and lower the reliability of exploiting them. ASLR, DEP/NX and SEHOP break classic memory-corruption techniques. Restricting ptrace, kernel pointer exposure, dmesg, unprivileged BPF and kexec removes common local-privilege-escalation primitives and information leaks. Hypervisor-enforced code integrity (HVCI) and VBS protect the kernel itself. These support SI-16 (memory protection), SC-39 (process isolation) and CM-6 baseline configuration.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1055 Process Injection; T1014 Rootkit; T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution

**Severity rationale:** CAT III: any vulnerability whose existence degrades measures to protect against loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001090**: Prevent unauthorized and unintended information transfer via shared system resources.  
  Rev 5: SC-4 · Rev 4: SC-4 · Rev 3: SC-4

### V-260473 · UBTU-22-213015 · CAT II: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS must disable kernel core dumps so that it can fail to a secure state if system initialization fails, shutdown fails or aborts fail.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-260473r1155207_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000184-GPOS-00078 |
| Topic | Kernel & Memory Exploit Mitigations, Boot Process & Console Security |
| CCI | CCI-001190 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-24 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-24 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SC-24 |
| Implemented via | Service (systemd) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must disable kernel core dumps so that it can fail to a secure state if system initialization fails, shutdown fails or aborts fail.

**Why it matters:** Hackers often break in by tricking a program into running their own instructions. These settings turn on built-in defenses that shuffle where things sit in memory and refuse to run code from places it shouldn't come from. It's like a bank regularly moving the vault around and refusing to accept instructions written on deposit slips.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Service | systemd | kdump-tools | mask |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
systemctl status kdump-tools.service
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
systemctl is-enabled kdump-tools; systemctl is-active kdump-tools
```

Expected: Expect masked / inactive.

**How it works:** Set kernel tunables in /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf and apply them with 'sysctl --system'. Boot parameters are added to GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX in /etc/default/grub, followed by 'update-grub' and a reboot. Disable core dumps through /etc/security/limits.conf ('* hard core 0') and /etc/systemd/coredump.conf.

**Also related (Boot Process & Console Security):** Create a GRUB superuser password hash with 'grub-mkpasswd-pbkdf2' and add 'set superusers="<name>"' and 'password_pbkdf2 <name> <hash>' to /etc/grub.d/40_custom (or 00_header), then run 'update-grub'. Kernel parameters go in GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX in /etc/default/grub, followed by 'update-grub'. Disable Ctrl-Alt-Delete with 'systemctl mask ctrl-alt-del.target' and 'systemctl daemon-reload'.

**Operational impact:** Restricting ptrace and dmesg affects debuggers (gdb, strace) for non-root users. Disabling core dumps removes crash diagnostics. HVCI can block older or unsigned drivers, so check driver compatibility first. Most sysctl changes are immediate, while boot parameters require a reboot.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify that kernel core dumps are disabled unless needed by using the following command:

$ systemctl status kdump-tools.service
o kdump-tools.service
     Loaded: masked (Reason: Unit kdump-tools.service is masked.)
     Active: inactive (dead)

If kdump-tools is not installed the output will be:
Unit kdump-tools.service could not be found.

If "kdump-tools.service" is not masked and inactive, ask the system administrator (SA) if the use of the service is required and documented with the information system security officer (ISSO).

If the service is active and is not documented, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
If kernel core dumps are not required, disable and mask "kdump-tools.service" by using the following command:

$ sudo systemctl mask kdump-tools --now

If kernel core dumps are required, document the need with the ISSO.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Kernel core dumps may contain the full contents of system memory at the time of the crash. Kernel core dumps may consume a considerable amount of disk space and may result in denial of service by exhausting the available space on the target file system partition.

**Threat & control context:** These mitigations don't remove vulnerabilities. They raise the cost and lower the reliability of exploiting them. ASLR, DEP/NX and SEHOP break classic memory-corruption techniques. Restricting ptrace, kernel pointer exposure, dmesg, unprivileged BPF and kexec removes common local-privilege-escalation primitives and information leaks. Hypervisor-enforced code integrity (HVCI) and VBS protect the kernel itself. These support SI-16 (memory protection), SC-39 (process isolation) and CM-6 baseline configuration.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1055 Process Injection; T1014 Rootkit; T1203 Exploitation for Client Execution; T1542 Pre-OS Boot; T1542.003 Pre-OS Boot: Bootkit; T1529 System Shutdown/Reboot

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001190**: Fail to an organization-defined known-system state for the list of organization-defined types of system failures on organization-defined system components on the indicated components while preserving organization-defined system state information in failure.  
  Rev 5: SC-24 · Rev 4: SC-24 · Rev 3: SC-24

### V-260476 · UBTU-22-214010 · CAT III: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS must be configured so that the Advance Package Tool (APT) prevents the installation of patches, service packs, device drivers, or operating system components without verification they have been digitally signed using a certificate that is recognized and approved by the organization.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-260476r1268241_rule` |
| Severity | CAT III (low) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000366-GPOS-00153 |
| Topic | Software & File Integrity Verification, Smart Card / PKI & Multifactor Authentication |
| CCI | CCI-003992, CCI-001749 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-14 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-5 (3) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Procedural / documentation |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured so that the Advance Package Tool (APT) prevents the installation of patches, service packs, device drivers, or operating system components without verification they have been digitally signed using a certificate that is recognized and approved by the organization.

**Why it matters:** This makes the computer check a digital "seal" on software before installing it, and keep a fingerprint of important files so it can notice if anyone changes them. It's like checking that a medicine bottle's safety seal is intact, and noticing straight away if someone has tampered with it.

**How important is it?** Low priority (CAT III): This setting adds an extra layer of protection. A gap here on its own is less likely to cause harm, but it weakens the overall defenses.

**Key terms:**
- *PKI / certificates*: Public Key Infrastructure: the system of digital ID certificates and trusted issuers.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Procedural / documentation. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep -i allowunauthenticated /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/*
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** APT verifies repository signatures with the keys in /etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d/ and per-source 'signed-by' keyrings, so never add '[trusted=yes]' or '--allow-unauthenticated'. Install AIDE with 'apt-get install aide aide-common', initialize with 'aideinit', and configure rules in /etc/aide/aide.conf. A daily check runs from /etc/cron.daily/dailyaidecheck. 'dpkg --verify' checks installed files against package checksums.

**Also related (Smart Card / PKI & Multifactor Authentication):** Ubuntu uses libpam-pkcs11 and opensc-pkcs11 for CAC/PIV login: a pam_pkcs11.so line in /etc/pam.d/common-auth, certificate mapping and OCSP/CRL policy in /etc/pam_pkcs11/pam_pkcs11.conf, and DoD CA certificates installed under /etc/ssl/certs (or /usr/local/share/ca-certificates followed by 'update-ca-certificates').

**Operational impact:** AIDE reports every legitimate change too, so re-baseline after approved patching and keep the database read-only or off-host. Internal repositories must sign their packages, or clients will refuse them.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify that APT is configured to prevent the installation of patches, service packs, device drivers, or Ubuntu operating system components without verification they have been digitally signed using a certificate that is recognized and approved by the organization by using the following command:

     $ grep -i allowunauthenticated /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/*
     /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/01-vendor-ubuntu:APT::Get::AllowUnauthenticated "false";

If "APT::Get::AllowUnauthenticated" is not set to "false", is commented out, or is missing, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure APT to prevent the installation of patches, service packs, device drivers, or Ubuntu operating system components without verification they have been digitally signed using a certificate that is recognized and approved by the organization.

Add or modify the following line in any file under the "/etc/apt/apt.conf.d/" directory:

APT::Get::AllowUnauthenticated "false";
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Changes to any software components can have significant effects on the overall security of the operating system. This requirement ensures the software has not been tampered with and that it has been provided by a trusted vendor.

Accordingly, patches, service packs, device drivers, or operating system components must be signed with a certificate recognized and approved by the organization.

Verifying the authenticity of the software prior to installation validates the integrity of the patch or upgrade received from a vendor. This ensures the software has not been tampered with and that it has been provided by a trusted vendor. Self-signed certificates are disallowed by this requirement. The operating system should not have to verify the software again. This requirement does not mandate DoW certificates for this purpose; however, the certificate used to verify the software must be from an approved certificate authority (CA).

**Threat & control context:** Signature verification ensures only vendor-authentic software is installed (CM-14 signed components, SI-7 software and information integrity). File-integrity monitoring such as AIDE detects unauthorized modification of binaries and configuration after the fact (SI-7(1), CM-3(5)), catching rootkits, backdoored binaries and configuration drift. The value of FIM depends on protecting the baseline database off-host and acting on alerts.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1195 Supply Chain Compromise; T1554 Compromise Host Software Binary; T1014 Rootkit; T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110 Brute Force; T1556 Modify Authentication Process

**Severity rationale:** CAT III: any vulnerability whose existence degrades measures to protect against loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-003992**: Prevent the installation of organization-defined software and firmware components without verification that the component has been digitally signed using a certificate that is recognized and approved by the organization.  
  Rev 5: CM-14 · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-001749**: The information system prevents the installation of organization-defined software components without verification the software component has been digitally signed using a certificate that is recognized and approved by the organization.  
  Rev 5: n/a · Rev 4: CM-5 (3) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-260477 · UBTU-22-214015 · CAT II: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS must be configured so that the Advance Package Tool (APT) removes all software components after updated versions have been installed.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-260477r1044773_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000437-GPOS-00194 |
| Topic | Least Functionality: Remove Unneeded Software |
| CCI | CCI-002617 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SI-2 (6) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SI-2 (6) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured so that the Advance Package Tool (APT) removes all software components after updated versions have been installed.

**Why it matters:** Every program on a computer is another possible way in for an attacker. This rule removes software the system doesn't need, especially old programs known to be unsafe. It's like clearing clutter out of a house: fewer things lying around means fewer things that can be broken or misused.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep -i remove-unused /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/50unattended-upgrades
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** Remove packages with 'apt-get remove --purge <pkg>' (purge also deletes their configuration files) and verify with 'dpkg -l | grep <pkg>'. Check what else 'apt' plans to remove before confirming the transaction.

**Operational impact:** Check that no application depends on the component before removing it (e.g. legacy scripts using PowerShell 2.0, tools that shell out to telnet or ftp). Keep a record of what was removed so it can be restored if a mission requirement is identified.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify APT is configured to remove all software components after updated versions have been installed by using the following command:

     $ grep -i remove-unused /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/50unattended-upgrades
     Unattended-Upgrade::Remove-Unused-Kernel-Packages "true";
     Unattended-Upgrade::Remove-Unused-Dependencies "true";

If "Unattended-Upgrade::Remove-Unused-Kernel-Packages" and "Unattended-Upgrade::Remove-Unused-Dependencies" are not set to "true", are commented out, or are missing, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure APT to remove all software components after updated versions have been installed.

Add or modify the following lines in the "/etc/apt/apt.conf.d/50unattended-upgrades" file:

Unattended-Upgrade::Remove-Unused-Kernel-Packages "true";
Unattended-Upgrade::Remove-Unused-Dependencies "true";
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Previous versions of software components that are not removed from the information system after updates have been installed may be exploited by adversaries. Some information technology products may remove older versions of software automatically from the information system.

**Threat & control context:** Every installed package, role and feature is potential attack surface, and some (telnet, rsh, TFTP, SMBv1, PowerShell 2.0) are inherently insecure or allow security controls to be bypassed. For example, PowerShell 2.0 bypasses script-block logging and AMSI. CM-7 (least functionality) and CM-7(1)/(2) require removing what isn't mission-necessary. Removal also reduces patch burden and false positives in vulnerability scans.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application; T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services; T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002617**: Remove previous versions of organization-defined software components after updated versions have been installed.  
  Rev 5: SI-2 (6) · Rev 4: SI-2 (6) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-260478 · UBTU-22-215010 · CAT II: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS must have the "libpam-pwquality" package installed.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-260478r991587_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00225 |
| Topic | Password Strength & Complexity |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Software package |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must have the "libpam-pwquality" package installed.

**Why it matters:** This sets the rules for how strong a password must be: long enough, and mixing capitals, lowercase letters, numbers and symbols. Short or simple passwords can be guessed by computers in seconds. A long, varied password is like a key with many unique notches that's much harder to copy.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *PAM*: Pluggable Authentication Modules: the Linux component that checks passwords and other sign-in requirements.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Package | apt | libpam-pwquality | Installed |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
dpkg -l | grep libpam-pwquality
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
dpkg -l libpam-pwquality 2>/dev/null | grep '^ii' || echo 'package libpam-pwquality is not installed'
```

Expected: Package must be installed.

**How it works:** Install libpam-pwquality ('apt-get install libpam-pwquality'), set minlen, dcredit/ucredit/lcredit/ocredit, difok, dictcheck and enforcing in /etc/security/pwquality.conf, and make sure /etc/pam.d/common-password calls pam_pwquality.so (with retry=3). Ubuntu manages the PAM stack with 'pam-auth-update'.

**Operational impact:** Takes effect at each user's next password change. Communicate the new requirements beforehand, and check that provisioning scripts and self-service reset portals can generate compliant passwords.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify Ubuntu 22.04 LTS has the "libpam-pwquality" package installed with  the following command:

     $ dpkg -l | grep libpam-pwquality
     ii     libpam-pwquality:amd64     1.4.4-1build2     amd64     PAM module to check password strength

If "libpam-pwquality" is not installed, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Install the "pam_pwquality" package by using the following command:

     $ sudo apt-get install libpam-pwquality
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Use of a complex password helps to increase the time and resources required to compromise the password. Password complexity, or strength, is a measure of the effectiveness of a password in resisting attempts at guessing and brute-force attacks. "pwquality" enforces complex password construction configuration and has the ability to limit brute-force attacks on the system.

**Threat & control context:** Length and composition rules raise the cost of both online guessing and offline cracking of captured hashes (IA-5(1)). DoD still requires a 15-character minimum with character-class rules, while NIST SP 800-63B now favors length plus breached-password screening over composition rules. Where the two conflict, the STIG governs for DoD systems. Note that complexity rules apply only when a password is changed, so assess the age of existing passwords too.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1110.002 Brute Force: Password Cracking; T1110.001 Brute Force: Password Guessing

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

### V-260479 · UBTU-22-215015 · CAT III: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS must have the "chrony" package installed.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-260479r1268251_rule` |
| Severity | CAT III (low) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Time Synchronization |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Software package |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must have the "chrony" package installed.

**Why it matters:** This keeps the computer's clock exactly in step with an official time source. That might sound minor, but security logs from different computers can only be pieced together if every clock agrees, and some sign-in systems refuse to work when clocks drift. It's like making sure all the witnesses' watches show the same time.

**How important is it?** Low priority (CAT III): This setting adds an extra layer of protection. A gap here on its own is less likely to cause harm, but it weakens the overall defenses.

**Key terms:**
- *NTP / chrony*: Network Time Protocol: how computers keep their clocks accurate over the network.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Package | apt | chrony | Installed |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
dpkg -l | grep chrony
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
dpkg -l chrony 2>/dev/null | grep '^ii' || echo 'package chrony is not installed'
```

Expected: Package must be installed.

**How it works:** Ubuntu uses chrony (or systemd-timesyncd by default on some releases). For chrony, configure /etc/chrony/chrony.conf with 'server <DoD-time-source> iburst maxpoll 16' and 'makestep 1 -1', and disable systemd-timesyncd so the two don't conflict. Verify with 'chronyc sources -v' and 'timedatectl'.

**Operational impact:** Large clock corrections can confuse running applications. chrony slews gradually by default. Make sure the time servers are reachable through the firewall (UDP 123).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the "chrony" package is installed using the following command:

     $ dpkg -l | grep chrony
     ii     chrony     4.2-2ubuntu2     amd64     Versatile implementation of the Network Time Protocol

If the "chrony" package is not installed, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Install the "chrony" network time protocol package using the following command:

     $ sudo apt-get install chrony
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Inaccurate time stamps make it more difficult to correlate events and can lead to an inaccurate analysis. Determining the correct time a particular event occurred on a system is critical when conducting forensic analysis and investigating system events. Sources outside the configured acceptable allowance (drift) may be inaccurate.

Organizations must consider endpoints that may not have regular access to the authoritative time server (e.g., mobile, teleworking, and tactical endpoints).

**Threat & control context:** Accurate, synchronized time underpins log correlation across systems, Kerberos authentication (5-minute skew tolerance), certificate validity checks and forensic timelines (AU-8, AU-8(1) synchronization with an authoritative source, AU-8(2) secondary source). Time sources should be authenticated where possible and restricted to client mode, so the host can't be abused as an NTP amplifier.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1070.006 Indicator Removal: Timestomp

**Severity rationale:** CAT III: any vulnerability whose existence degrades measures to protect against loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

**Also related (Time Synchronization):** Ubuntu uses chrony (or systemd-timesyncd by default on some releases). For chrony, configure /etc/chrony/chrony.conf with 'server <DoD-time-source> iburst maxpoll 16' and 'makestep 1 -1', and disable systemd-timesyncd so the two don't conflict. Verify with 'chronyc sources -v' and 'timedatectl'.

```text

Removal also reduces patch burden and false positives in vulnerability scans.

```text
Configure the Ubuntu operating system to disable nonessential capabilities by removing the nfs-kernel-server package from the system with the following commands:

Remove packages if present:
$ sudo apt purge --yes nfs-kernel-server

Remove any unneeded dependencies:
$ sudo apt autoremove --yes

Verify that NFS services are gone:
$ sudo systemctl list-units --type=service | grep nfs
```

### V-260484 · UBTU-22-231010 · CAT I: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS must implement cryptographic mechanisms to prevent unauthorized disclosure and modification of all information that requires protection at rest.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-260484r1261427_rule` |
| Severity | CAT I (high) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000185-GPOS-00079 |
| Topic | Data-at-Rest Encryption |
| CCI | CCI-001199, CCI-002475, CCI-002476 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-28, SC-28 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-28, SC-28 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SC-28 |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must implement cryptographic mechanisms to prevent unauthorized disclosure and modification of all information that requires protection at rest.

**Why it matters:** This scrambles everything stored on the computer's drive so it can only be read after the right key or PIN is entered at startup. If someone steals the laptop or pulls out the hard drive, all they get is gibberish. It's like keeping your documents in a locked safe instead of a cardboard box.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
fdisk -l
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
more /etc/crypttab
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** Ubuntu uses LUKS (dm-crypt) for block-device encryption, normally chosen at install time ('Encrypt the new Ubuntu installation'). Retrofitting encryption to an existing root volume generally requires a rebuild. Verify with 'lsblk -f' or 'cryptsetup status <mapping>'.

**Operational impact:** Requiring a pre-boot PIN means unattended reboots (patch windows, remote power-cycles) stop at the PIN prompt unless Network Unlock is deployed. Plan key escrow and helpdesk recovery procedures before rollout.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify Ubuntu 22.04 LTS prevents unauthorized disclosure or modification of all information requiring at-rest protection by using disk encryption.

Note: If there is a documented and approved reason for not having data-at-rest encryption, this requirement is not applicable.

Determine the partition layout for the system by using the following command:

     $ sudo fdisk -l

     ...
     Device               Start               End        Sectors       Size  Type
     /dev/sda1         2048      2203647       2201600          1G  EFI System
     /dev/sda2  2203648      6397951       4194304          2G  Linux filesystem
     /dev/sda3  6397952  536868863  530470912  252.9G  Linux filesystem
     ...

Verify the system partitions are all encrypted by using the following command:

     # more /etc/crypttab

Every persistent disk partition present must have an entry in the file.

If any partitions other than the boot partition or pseudo file systems (such as /proc or /sys) are not listed, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
To encrypt an entire partition, dedicate a partition for encryption in the partition layout.

Note: Encrypting a partition in an already-installed system is more difficult because it will need to be resized and existing partitions changed.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Operating systems handling data requiring "data at rest" protections must employ cryptographic mechanisms to prevent unauthorized disclosure and modification of the information at rest.

Selection of a cryptographic mechanism is based on the need to protect the integrity of organizational information. The strength of the mechanism is commensurate with the security category and/or classification of the information. Organizations have the flexibility to either encrypt all information on storage devices (i.e., full disk encryption) or encrypt specific data structures (e.g., files, records, or fields).

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000185-GPOS-00079, SRG-OS-000404-GPOS-00183, SRG-OS-000405-GPOS-00184

**Threat & control context:** Full-volume encryption protects confidentiality when an adversary gains physical possession of storage, an attack path that bypasses every OS-level access control. Pre-boot authentication (TPM + PIN) defends against cold-boot, DMA and TPM-sniffing attacks that defeat TPM-only configurations. Maps primarily to SC-28 (Protection of Information at Rest). Assess key escrow and recovery procedures as well, because an unrecoverable key is an availability risk.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1005 Data from Local System; T1200 Hardware Additions; T1552 Unsecured Credentials

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001199**: Protects the confidentiality and/or integrity of organization-defined information at rest.  
  Rev 5: SC-28 · Rev 4: SC-28 · Rev 3: SC-28
- **CCI-002475**: Implement cryptographic mechanisms to prevent unauthorized modification of organization-defined information at rest on organization-defined system components.  
  Rev 5: SC-28 (1) · Rev 4: SC-28 (1) · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-002476**: Implement cryptographic mechanisms to prevent unauthorized disclosure of organization-defined information at rest on organization-defined system components.  
  Rev 5: SC-28 (1) · Rev 4: SC-28 (1) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-260485 · UBTU-22-232010 · CAT II: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS must have directories that contain system commands set to a mode of "755" or less permissive.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-260485r991559_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000258-GPOS-00099 |
| Topic | File & Directory Permissions |
| CCI | CCI-001495 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-9 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-9 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-9 |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must have directories that contain system commands set to a mode of "755" or less permissive.

**Why it matters:** Every file on a computer has a label saying who owns it and who can read or change it. This rule makes sure sensitive files, such as the list of password fingerprints or system settings, can only be touched by the right people. It's like keeping personnel files in a locked HR cabinet rather than on the break-room table.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
find /bin /sbin /usr/bin /usr/sbin /usr/local/bin /usr/local/sbin -perm /022 -type d -exec stat -c "%n %a" '{}' \;
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** Check mode and ownership with 'stat -c "%a %U %G %n" <path>' and fix them with 'chmod', 'chown' and 'chgrp'. Find unowned files with 'find / -xdev -nouser -o -nogroup'. Default permissions for new files come from UMASK in /etc/login.defs. 'dpkg --verify' highlights packaged files that have changed.

**Operational impact:** Tightening permissions can break applications that read their configuration as a non-root user. Prefer group-based access over loosening the mode, and re-check after package updates, which can reset modes.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the system commands directories have mode "755" or less permissive by using the following command:

     $ find /bin /sbin /usr/bin /usr/sbin /usr/local/bin /usr/local/sbin -perm /022 -type d -exec stat -c "%n %a" '{}' \;

If any directories are found to be group-writable or world-writable, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure Ubuntu 22.04 LTS commands directories to be protected from unauthorized access. Run the following command:

     $ sudo find /bin /sbin /usr/bin /usr/sbin /usr/local/bin /usr/local/sbin -perm /022 -type d -exec chmod -R 755 '{}' \;
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Protecting audit information also includes identifying and protecting the tools used to view and manipulate log data. Therefore, protecting audit tools is necessary to prevent unauthorized operation on audit information.

Operating systems providing tools to interface with audit information will leverage user permissions and roles identifying the user accessing the tools and the corresponding rights the user has in order to make access decisions regarding the deletion of audit tools.

Audit tools include, but are not limited to, vendor-provided and open source audit tools needed to successfully view and manipulate audit information system activity and records. Audit tools include custom queries and report generators.

**Threat & control context:** Permissive ownership or modes on credentials (shadow, SSH host keys), libraries, system binaries, cron and boot configuration, and log files allow tampering, credential theft and execution-flow hijacking. This is AC-3 / AC-6 least privilege applied at the file-system layer, plus CM-5(6) (privilege to change software libraries). Unowned files and world-writable directories without the sticky bit are common persistence and escalation footholds.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1222 File and Directory Permissions Modification; T1574 Hijack Execution Flow; T1548.001 Abuse Elevation Control: Setuid and Setgid

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001495**: Protect audit tools from unauthorized deletion.  
  Rev 5: AU-9 a · Rev 4: AU-9 · Rev 3: AU-9

     $ sudo chmod 0755 /var/log
```

The structure and content of error messages must be carefully considered by the organization and development team. The extent to which the information system is able to identify and handle error conditions is guided by organizational policy and operational requirements.

**Threat & control context:** Permissive ownership or modes on credentials (shadow, SSH host keys), libraries, system binaries, cron and boot configuration, and log files allow tampering, credential theft and execution-flow hijacking. This is AC-3 / AC-6 least privilege applied at the file-system layer, plus CM-5(6) (privilege to change software libraries). ### V-260489 · UBTU-22-232026 · CAT II: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS must generate error messages that provide information necessary for corrective actions without revealing information that could be exploited by adversaries.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-260489r1134796_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000205-GPOS-00083 |
| Topic | Audit Log & Tool Protection |
| CCI | CCI-001312 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SI-11 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SI-11 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SI-11 b |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must generate error messages that provide information necessary for corrective actions without revealing information that could be exploited by adversaries.

**Why it matters:** The security diary is only useful if nobody can secretly edit or tear pages out of it. This rule locks down who can read or change the logs and the tools that manage them. It's like keeping the security camera footage in a locked room that only a couple of trusted people can enter.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
find /var/log -perm /137 ! -name '*[bw]tmp' ! -name '*lastlog' -type f -exec stat -c "%n %a" {} \;
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** On Ubuntu, audit logs live under /var/log/audit/ (mode 0600 or 0640, owned by root, group per log_group). Audit tools are /sbin/auditctl, aureport, ausearch, autrace, auditd, rsyslogd and augenrules (mode 0755, owned by root). '-e 2' at the end of the rules makes the configuration immutable until reboot, and '--loginuid-immutable' prevents processes from changing their audit login UID.

**Operational impact:** With '-e 2', any later audit rule change requires a reboot to take effect, so schedule audit rule updates in maintenance windows.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify Ubuntu 22.04 LTS has all system log files under the "/var/log" directory with a permission set to "640" or less permissive by using the following command:

Note: The btmp, wtmp, and lastlog files are excluded. Refer to the Discussion for details.

     $ sudo find /var/log -perm /137 ! -name '*[bw]tmp' ! -name '*lastlog' -type f -exec stat -c "%n %a" {} \;

If the command displays any output, this is a finding.

Note: If output regarding history.log or eipp.log.xz is displayed, this is not a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure Ubuntu 22.04 LTS to set permissions of all log files under the "/var/log" directory to "640" or more restricted by using the following command:

Note: The btmp, wtmp, and lastlog files are excluded. Refer to the Discussion for details.

     $ sudo find /var/log -perm /137 ! -name '*[bw]tmp' ! -name '*lastlog' -type f -exec chmod 640 '{}' \;
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Any operating system providing too much information in error messages risks compromising the data and security of the structure, and organizations must carefully consider the content and structure of error messages.

The extent to which information systems are able to identify and handle error conditions is guided by organizational policy and operational requirements. Information that could be exploited by adversaries includes, for example, erroneous logon attempts with passwords entered by mistake as the username, mission/business information that can be derived from (if not stated explicitly by) information recorded, and personal information, such as account numbers, Social Security numbers, and credit card numbers.

The /var/log/btmp, /var/log/wtmp, and /var/log/lastlog files have group write and global read permissions to allow for the lastlog function to perform. Limiting the permissions beyond this configuration will result in the failure of functions that rely on the lastlog database.

**Threat & control context:** If a non-privileged user, or an attacker running as one, can read, alter or delete audit data or reconfigure the audit subsystem, the audit trail loses its evidentiary value. AU-9 (protection of audit information) together with AU-9(3) (cryptographic protection) and AU-9(4) (access by subset of privileged users) require restrictive ownership and modes on logs and tools, integrity verification of audit binaries (via AIDE), and immutable audit rules ('-e 2') so the rule set can't be changed without a reboot.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1070.002 Indicator Removal: Clear Linux or Mac System Logs; T1070.001 Indicator Removal: Clear Windows Event Logs; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001312**: Generate error messages that provide information necessary for corrective actions without revealing information that could be exploited.  
  Rev 5: SI-11 a · Rev 4: SI-11 a · Rev 3: SI-11 b

### V-260490 · UBTU-22-232027 · CAT II: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS must generate system journal entries without revealing information that could be exploited by adversaries.

| Topic | Audit Log Capacity, Offloading & Failure Handling |
| CCI | CCI-001312 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SI-11 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SI-11 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SI-11 b |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must generate system journal entries without revealing information that could be exploited by adversaries.

**Why it matters:** The computer keeps a "security diary" of important events. This rule makes sure the diary has enough pages, that a copy is sent to a separate, safe location, and that someone is alerted if the diary fills up or stops working. It's like a store's security cameras recording to an off-site server so a thief can't simply take the tape.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *root*: The all-powerful administrator account on Linux.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
find /run/log/journal /var/log/journal -type d -exec stat -c "%n %a" {} \;
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
find /run/log/journal /var/log/journal  -type f -exec stat -c "%n %a" {} \;
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** auditd capacity and failure behavior are set in /etc/audit/auditd.conf (space_left, space_left_action, disk_full_action, action_mail_acct). Off-load with audisp-remote (package audispd-plugins, configured in /etc/audit/audisp-remote.conf or plugins.d/au-remote.conf) or forward with rsyslog. Install auditd with 'apt-get install auditd audispd-plugins'.

**Operational impact:** Actions such as 'halt' or 'single' on disk-full prioritize integrity over availability and can take a production system down. Agree the action with the ISSO/AO and monitor free space proactively. Larger local logs consume disk; forwarding requires network connectivity and certificates for TLS.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the /run/log/journal and /var/log/journal directories have permissions set to "2750" or less permissive by using the following command:

$ sudo find /run/log/journal /var/log/journal -type d -exec stat -c "%n %a" {} \;
/run/log/journal 2750
/var/log/journal 2750
/var/log/journal/3b018e681c904487b11671b9c1987cce 2750

If any output returned has a permission set greater than "2750", this is a finding.

Verify all files in the /run/log/journal and /var/log/journal directories have permissions set to "640" or less permissive by using the following command:

     $ sudo find /run/log/journal /var/log/journal  -type f -exec stat -c "%n %a" {} \;
     /var/log/journal/3b018e681c904487b11671b9c1987cce/system@99dcc72bb1134aaeae4bf157aa7606f4-0000000000003c7a-0006073f8d1c0fec.journal 640
     /var/log/journal/3b018e681c904487b11671b9c1987cce/system.journal 640
     /var/log/journal/3b018e681c904487b11671b9c1987cce/user-1000.journal 640
     /var/log/journal/3b018e681c904487b11671b9c1987cce/user-1000@bdedf14602ff4081a77dc7a6debc8626-00000000000062a6-00060b4b414b617a.journal 640
     /var/log/journal/3b018e681c904487b11671b9c1987cce

If any output returned has a permission set greater than "640", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure Ubuntu 22.04 LTS to set the appropriate permissions to the files and directories used by the systemd journal:

Add or modify the following lines in the "`/usr/lib/tmpfiles.d/systemd.conf" file:
z /run/log/journal 2750 root systemd-journal - -
Z /run/log/journal/%m ~2750 root systemd-journal - -
z /var/log/journal 2750 root systemd-journal - -
z /var/log/journal/%m 2750 root systemd-journal - -
z /var/log/journal/%m/system.journal 0640 root systemd-journal - -

Restart the system for the changes to take effect.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Any operating system providing too much information in error messages risks compromising the data and security of the structure, and content of error messages needs to be carefully considered by the organization.

Organizations carefully consider the structure/content of error messages. The extent to which information systems are able to identify and handle error conditions is guided by organizational policy and operational requirements. Information that could be exploited by adversaries includes, for example, erroneous logon attempts with passwords entered by mistake as the username, mission/business information that can be derived from (if not stated explicitly by) information recorded, and personal information, such as account numbers, social security numbers, and credit card numbers.

**Threat & control context:** Logs that roll over, fill the disk or exist only on the compromised host can't support incident response. Attackers routinely clear or flood local logs. AU-4 (storage capacity), AU-4(1) (transfer to alternate storage), AU-5 (response to processing failures) and AU-9(2) (backup onto a separate system) require sized local storage, real-time off-host forwarding, and defined behavior (alert, halt or single-user) when audit capability is lost. Validate end-to-end delivery at the SIEM, not just the client configuration.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1070 Indicator Removal; T1562.006 Impair Defenses: Indicator Blocking

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001312**: Generate error messages that provide information necessary for corrective actions without revealing information that could be exploited.  
  Rev 5: SI-11 a · Rev 4: SI-11 a · Rev 3: SI-11 b

### V-260491 · UBTU-22-232030 · CAT II: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS must configure "/var/log/syslog" file with mode "640" or less permissive.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-260491r958566_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000206-GPOS-00084 |
| Topic | Audit Log Capacity, Offloading & Failure Handling, File & Directory Permissions |
| CCI | CCI-001314 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SI-11 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SI-11 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SI-11 c |
| Implemented via | File permission / ownership / label |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must configure "/var/log/syslog" file with mode "640" or less permissive.

**Why it matters:** The computer keeps a "security diary" of important events. This rule makes sure the diary has enough pages, that a copy is sent to a separate, safe location, and that someone is alerted if the diary fills up or stops working. It's like a store's security cameras recording to an off-site server so a thief can't simply take the tape.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Permission | chmod | 0640 /var/log/syslog |  |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
stat -c "%n %a" /var/log/syslog
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo stat -c '%a %U %G %n' /var/log/syslog
```

Expected: Mode/owner/group must match: chmod 0640 /var/log/syslog.

**How it works:** auditd capacity and failure behavior are set in /etc/audit/auditd.conf (space_left, space_left_action, disk_full_action, action_mail_acct). Off-load with audisp-remote (package audispd-plugins, configured in /etc/audit/audisp-remote.conf or plugins.d/au-remote.conf) or forward with rsyslog. Install auditd with 'apt-get install auditd audispd-plugins'.

**Also related (File & Directory Permissions):** Check mode and ownership with 'stat -c "%a %U %G %n" <path>' and fix them with 'chmod', 'chown' and 'chgrp'. Find unowned files with 'find / -xdev -nouser -o -nogroup'. Default permissions for new files come from UMASK in /etc/login.defs. 'dpkg --verify' highlights packaged files that have changed.

**Operational impact:** Actions such as 'halt' or 'single' on disk-full prioritize integrity over availability and can take a production system down. Agree the action with the ISSO/AO and monitor free space proactively. Larger local logs consume disk; forwarding requires network connectivity and certificates for TLS.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify that Ubuntu 22.04 LTS configures the "/var/log/syslog" file with mode "640" or less permissive by using the following command:

     $ stat -c "%n %a" /var/log/syslog
     /var/log/syslog 640

If a value of "640" or less permissive is not returned, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure Ubuntu 22.04 LTS to have permissions of "640" for the "/var/log/syslog" file by using the following command:

     $ sudo chmod 0640 /var/log/syslog
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Only authorized personnel should be aware of errors and the details of the errors. Error messages are an indicator of an organization's operational state or can identify the operating system or platform. Additionally, personally identifiable information (PII) and operational information must not be revealed through error messages to unauthorized personnel or their designated representatives.

The structure and content of error messages must be carefully considered by the organization and development team. The extent to which the information system is able to identify and handle error conditions is guided by organizational policy and operational requirements.

**Threat & control context:** Logs that roll over, fill the disk or exist only on the compromised host can't support incident response. Attackers routinely clear or flood local logs. AU-4 (storage capacity), AU-4(1) (transfer to alternate storage), AU-5 (response to processing failures) and AU-9(2) (backup onto a separate system) require sized local storage, real-time off-host forwarding, and defined behavior (alert, halt or single-user) when audit capability is lost. Validate end-to-end delivery at the SIEM, not just the client configuration.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1070 Indicator Removal; T1562.006 Impair Defenses: Indicator Blocking; T1222 File and Directory Permissions Modification; T1574 Hijack Execution Flow; T1548.001 Abuse Elevation Control: Setuid and Setgid

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001314**: Reveal error messages only to organization-defined personnel or roles.
