### V-260537 · UBTU-22-271020 · CAT II: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS must retain a user's session lock until that user reestablishes access using established identification and authentication procedures.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-260537r1069101_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000028-GPOS-00009 |
| Topic | Session Lock & Inactivity Timeout |
| CCI | CCI-000056 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-11 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-11 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-11 b |
| Implemented via | GNOME (dconf) setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must retain a user's session lock until that user reestablishes access using established identification and authentication procedures.

**Why it matters:** If you walk away from the computer and forget to lock it, it will lock itself after a short time (15 minutes for DoD) and hide what was on the screen. Anyone who sits down then has to sign in again. It's like a car that locks its doors automatically when you walk away.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *GNOME / dconf*: The Linux desktop environment and its settings database.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| dconf | [org/gnome/desktop/screensaver] | lock-enabled | true |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
gsettings get org.gnome.desktop.screensaver lock-enabled
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
grep -rs '^[[:space:]]*lock-enabled' /etc/dconf/db/*.d/
```

Expected: lock-enabled=true under [org/gnome/desktop/screensaver].

**How it works:** Set GNOME locking through dconf (org/gnome/desktop/screensaver lock-enabled=true, org/gnome/desktop/session idle-delay=uint32 900) with matching locks, followed by 'dconf update'. For console sessions, install 'vlock' so users can lock a terminal, and set TMOUT=900 (readonly) in /etc/profile.d/. SSH idle termination uses ClientAliveInterval/CountMax.

**Operational impact:** Users running long unattended interactive jobs may be disconnected. Kiosk or operations displays that must stay visible need a documented exception and compensating physical controls.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify Ubuntu 22.04 LTS has a graphical user interface session lock enabled by using the following command:

Note: If no graphical user interface is installed, this requirement is not applicable.

     $ sudo gsettings get org.gnome.desktop.screensaver lock-enabled
     true

If "lock-enabled" is not set to "true", is commented out, or is missing, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure Ubuntu 22.04 LTS to allow a user to lock the current graphical user interface session.

Create or edit a file named /etc/dconf/db/local.d/00-screensaver with the following contents:

[org/gnome/desktop/screensaver]
lock-enabled=true
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** A session lock is a temporary action taken when a user stops work and moves away from the immediate physical vicinity of the information system but does not want to log out because of the temporary nature of the absence.

The session lock is implemented at the point where session activity can be determined.

Regardless of where the session lock is determined and implemented, once invoked, a session lock of Ubuntu 22.04 LTS must remain in place until the user reauthenticates. No other activity aside from reauthentication must unlock the system.

**Threat & control context:** Unattended, unlocked sessions are an opportunistic access path for insiders and visitors, so physical access becomes logical access. AC-11 (device lock, 15 minutes in DoD), AC-11(1) (pattern-hiding displays) and AC-12 (session termination) require automatic locking that the user can't override, re-authentication to unlock, and concealment of on-screen content. Smart-card removal locking extends this to CAC workflows.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000056**: Retain the device lock until the user reestablishes access using established identification and authentication procedures.  
  Rev 5: AC-11 b · Rev 4: AC-11 b · Rev 3: AC-11 b

### V-260539 · UBTU-22-271030 · CAT I: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS must disable the x86 Ctrl-Alt-Delete key sequence if a graphical user interface is installed.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-260539r1268251_rule` |
| Severity | CAT I (high) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Boot Process & Console Security, Logon Screen & Desktop Settings |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | GNOME (dconf) setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must disable the x86 Ctrl-Alt-Delete key sequence if a graphical user interface is installed.

**Why it matters:** While a computer is starting up, before the normal sign-in screen appears, there are special "maintenance doors" that can skip the usual security. This rule puts locks on those doors and makes sure the computer only starts with trusted software, like making sure nobody can hot-wire a car by tampering with it before the key is turned.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

**Key terms:**
- *GNOME / dconf*: The Linux desktop environment and its settings database.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| dconf | [org/gnome/settings-daemon/plugins/media-keys] | logout | @as [] |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
gsettings get org.gnome.settings-daemon.plugins.media-keys logout
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
grep -rs '^[[:space:]]*logout' /etc/dconf/db/*.d/
```

Expected: logout=@as [] under [org/gnome/settings-daemon/plugins/media-keys].

**How it works:** Create a GRUB superuser password hash with 'grub-mkpasswd-pbkdf2' and add 'set superusers="<name>"' and 'password_pbkdf2 <name> <hash>' to /etc/grub.d/40_custom (or 00_header), then run 'update-grub'. Kernel parameters go in GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX in /etc/default/grub, followed by 'update-grub'. Disable Ctrl-Alt-Delete with 'systemctl mask ctrl-alt-del.target' and 'systemctl daemon-reload'.

**Also related (Logon Screen & Desktop Settings):** On Ubuntu, GDM3 settings live in /etc/gdm3/ (for example 'AutomaticLoginEnable=false' in /etc/gdm3/custom.conf), and GNOME policy is managed through dconf databases in /etc/dconf/db/local.d/ with locks, followed by 'dconf update'. If no GUI is required, remove the desktop packages and set 'systemctl set-default multi-user.target'.

**Operational impact:** Store the boot-loader password in the system's credential vault, because you'll need it for kernel-parameter troubleshooting. Converting Legacy BIOS installs to UEFI generally requires MBR2GPT or a rebuild.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify Ubuntu 22.04 LTS is not configured to reboot the system when Ctrl-Alt-Delete is pressed when using a graphical user interface by using the following command:

Note: If no graphical user interface is installed, this requirement is not applicable.

     $ gsettings get org.gnome.settings-daemon.plugins.media-keys logout
     @as []

If the "logout" key is bound to an action, is commented out, or is missing, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure Ubuntu 22.04 LTS to disable the Ctrl-Alt-Delete sequence when using a graphical user interface.

Create or edit a file named /etc/dconf/db/local.d/00-mediakeys with the following contents:

[org/gnome/settings-daemon/plugins/media-keys]
logout=@as []

Update the dconf settings:

$ sudo dconf update
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** A locally logged-on user who presses Ctrl-Alt-Delete, when at the console, can reboot the system. If accidentally pressed, as could happen in the case of a mixed OS environment, this can create the risk of short-term loss of availability of systems due to unintentional reboot. In the graphical environment, risk of unintentional reboot from the Ctrl-Alt-Delete sequence is reduced because the user will be prompted before any action is taken.

**Threat & control context:** Anyone with console or hypervisor access can interrupt the boot process to edit kernel parameters (e.g. 'init=/bin/bash'), boot into single-user or rescue mode, or load an untrusted boot loader, bypassing all OS authentication. A boot-loader password, authenticated rescue modes and UEFI Secure Boot close this path (AC-3, CM-6, SI-7(9) boot process integrity). Disabling Ctrl-Alt-Del and similar console actions prevents accidental or malicious reboots (availability).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1542 Pre-OS Boot; T1542.003 Pre-OS Boot: Bootkit; T1529 System Shutdown/Reboot; T1087 Account Discovery; T1078 Valid Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

### V-260540 · UBTU-22-291010 · CAT II: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS must disable automatic mounting of Universal Serial Bus (USB) mass storage driver.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-260540r986276_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000378-GPOS-00163 |
| Topic | Removable Media, Peripherals & Wireless, File System Layout & Mount Options |
| CCI | CCI-001958, CCI-003959 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-3, CM-7 (9) (b) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must disable automatic mounting of Universal Serial Bus (USB) mass storage driver.

**Why it matters:** USB sticks, Bluetooth and Wi-Fi are convenient, but they're also easy ways for a virus to sneak in or for data to sneak out. This rule turns off or tightly controls these connections. It's like a secure office that doesn't let visitors plug unknown devices into its computers.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *USB*: The common plug used for thumb drives, keyboards and many other devices.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep usb-storage /etc/modprobe.d/* | grep "/bin/false"
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep usb-storage /etc/modprobe.d/* | grep -i "blacklist"
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** Block USB storage with 'install usb-storage /bin/false' and 'blacklist usb-storage' in /etc/modprobe.d/*.conf, and check with 'modprobe -n -v usb-storage'. Disable wireless interfaces with 'nmcli radio all off' or by blacklisting their driver modules. USBGuard is available from the Ubuntu archive ('apt-get install usbguard').

**Also related (File System Layout & Mount Options):** On Ubuntu, partitions are defined at install time (/home, /tmp, /var, /var/log, /var/log/audit, /var/tmp). Changing them later generally needs LVM work or a rebuild. Mount options go in /etc/fstab (e.g. 'defaults,nodev,nosuid,noexec') and are applied with 'mount -o remount <mountpoint>'. Verify with 'findmnt -no OPTIONS <mountpoint>'. Disable autofs ('systemctl disable --now autofs') unless it's required.

**Operational impact:** Blocking USB storage affects users who move data on thumb drives, so provide an approved transfer method. Make sure USBGuard policies allow keyboards, mice and smart card readers before enforcing, or you may lose console input.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify Ubuntu 22.04 LTS disables ability to load the USB storage kernel module by using the following command:

     $ grep usb-storage /etc/modprobe.d/* | grep "/bin/false"
     /etc/modprobe.d/stig.conf:install usb-storage /bin/false

If the command does not return any output, or the line is commented out, this is a finding.

Verify Ubuntu 22.04 LTS disables the ability to use USB mass storage device.

     $ grep usb-storage /etc/modprobe.d/* | grep -i "blacklist"
     /etc/modprobe.d/stig.conf:blacklist usb-storage

If the command does not return any output, or the line is commented out, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure Ubuntu 22.04 LTS to disable using the USB storage kernel module.

Create and/or append a custom file under "/etc/modprobe.d/" to contain the following:

     $ sudo su -c "echo install usb-storage /bin/false >> /etc/modprobe.d/stig.conf"

Configure Ubuntu 22.04 LTS to disable the ability to use USB mass storage devices.

     $ sudo su -c "echo blacklist usb-storage >> /etc/modprobe.d/stig.conf"
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without authenticating devices, unidentified or unknown devices may be introduced, thereby facilitating malicious activity.

Peripherals include, but are not limited to, such devices as flash drives, external storage, and printers.

**Threat & control context:** Removable media and peripheral interfaces bypass network-layer defenses. They enable malware introduction (AutoRun worms, BadUSB, HID injection), data exfiltration, and DMA attacks via Thunderbolt or FireWire. Wireless radios add unmanaged network paths. These settings implement MP-7 (media use), AC-18/AC-19 (wireless and mobile device access) and CM-7 (least functionality) and should be paired with device-control allowlisting (USBGuard, Windows device installation restrictions).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1091 Replication Through Removable Media; T1052.001 Exfiltration Over USB; T1200 Hardware Additions; T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1499 Endpoint Denial of Service

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001958**: Authenticate organization-defined devices and/or types of devices before establishing a local, remote, and/or network connection.  
  Rev 5: IA-3 · Rev 4: IA-3 · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-003959**: Prohibit the use or connection of unauthorized hardware components.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 (9) (b) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a

### V-260541 · UBTU-22-291015 · CAT II: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS must disable all wireless network adapters.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-260541r1268254_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000481-GPOS-00481 |
| Topic | Removable Media, Peripherals & Wireless |
| CCI | CCI-002418 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-8 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-8 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must disable all wireless network adapters.

**Why it matters:** USB sticks, Bluetooth and Wi-Fi are convenient, but they're also easy ways for a virus to sneak in or for data to sneak out. This rule turns off or tightly controls these connections. It's like a secure office that doesn't let visitors plug unknown devices into its computers.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
cat /proc/net/wireless
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** Block USB storage with 'install usb-storage /bin/false' and 'blacklist usb-storage' in /etc/modprobe.d/*.conf, and check with 'modprobe -n -v usb-storage'. Disable wireless interfaces with 'nmcli radio all off' or by blacklisting their driver modules. USBGuard is available from the Ubuntu archive ('apt-get install usbguard').

**Operational impact:** Blocking USB storage affects users who move data on thumb drives, so provide an approved transfer method. Make sure USBGuard policies allow keyboards, mice and smart card readers before enforcing, or you may lose console input.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify that there are no wireless interfaces configured on the system by using the following command:

Note: If the system does not have any physical wireless network radios, this requirement is not applicable.

     $ cat /proc/net/wireless

If any wireless interface names are listed under "Interface" and have not been documented and approved by the information system security officer (ISSO), this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Disable all wireless network interfaces by using the following command:

     $ sudo ifdown <wireless_interface_name>

For each interface listed, find their respective module by using the following command:

     $ basename $(readlink -f /sys/class/net/<wireless_interface_name>/device/driver)

where <wireless_interface_name> must be substituted by the actual interface name.

Create and/or append a custom file under "/etc/modprobe.d/" by using the following command:

     $ sudo su -c "echo install <module_name> /bin/false >> /etc/modprobe.d/stig.conf"

where <module_name> must be substituted by the actual module name.

For each module from the system, execute the following command to remove it:

     $ sudo modprobe -r <module_name>
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Without protection of communications with wireless peripherals, confidentiality and integrity may be compromised because unprotected communications can be intercepted and either read, altered, or used to compromise the operating system.

This requirement applies to wireless peripheral technologies (e.g., wireless mice, keyboards, displays, etc.) used with an operating system. Wireless peripherals (e.g., Wi-Fi/Bluetooth/IR Keyboards, Mice, and Pointing Devices and Near Field Communications [NFC]) present a unique challenge by creating an open, unsecured port on a computer. Wireless peripherals must meet DoW requirements for wireless data transmission and be approved for use by the AO. Even though some wireless peripherals, such as mice and pointing devices, do not ordinarily carry information that need to be protected, modification of communications with these wireless peripherals may be used to compromise the operating system. Communication paths outside the physical protection of a controlled boundary are exposed to the possibility of interception and modification.

Protecting the confidentiality and integrity of communications with wireless peripherals can be accomplished by physical means (e.g., employing physical barriers to wireless radio frequencies) or by logical means (e.g., employing cryptographic techniques). If physical means of protection are employed, then logical means (cryptography) do not have to be employed, and vice versa. If the wireless peripheral is only passing telemetry data, encryption of the data may not be required.

**Threat & control context:** Removable media and peripheral interfaces bypass network-layer defenses. They enable malware introduction (AutoRun worms, BadUSB, HID injection), data exfiltration, and DMA attacks via Thunderbolt or FireWire. Wireless radios add unmanaged network paths. These settings implement MP-7 (media use), AC-18/AC-19 (wireless and mobile device access) and CM-7 (least functionality) and should be paired with device-control allowlisting (USBGuard, Windows device installation restrictions).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1091 Replication Through Removable Media; T1052.001 Exfiltration Over USB; T1200 Hardware Additions

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002418**: Protect the confidentiality and/or integrity of transmitted information.  
  Rev 5: SC-8 · Rev 4: SC-8 · Rev 3: n/a

### V-260542 · UBTU-22-411010 · CAT II: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS must prevent direct login into the root account.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-260542r1015006_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000109-GPOS-00056 |
| Topic | Built-in & Privileged Account Hardening |
| CCI | CCI-004045, CCI-000770 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-2 (5) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-2 (5) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-2 (5) (b) |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must prevent direct login into the root account.

**Why it matters:** Every computer comes with a few built-in "master" accounts whose names everyone knows. This rule makes those accounts harder to abuse, for example by not letting anyone log in directly as the master account and never allowing accounts with no password. It's like not leaving the master key labelled "MASTER KEY" hanging by the front door.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *root*: The all-powerful administrator account on Linux.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
passwd -S root
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** Lock the root password ('passwd -l root') so administrators work through sudo, set 'PermitRootLogin no' and 'PermitEmptyPasswords no' for sshd, and remove 'nullok' from pam_unix in /etc/pam.d/common-auth and common-password so empty passwords are rejected.

**Operational impact:** Make sure at least one named administrator account with sudo or admin rights works before disabling root or Administrator logon paths. Renaming the built-in Administrator can break scripts that reference it by name.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify Ubuntu 22.04 LTS prevents direct logins to the root account by using the following command:

     $ sudo passwd -S root
     root L 08/09/2022 0 99999 7 -1

If the output does not contain "L" in the second field to indicate the account is locked, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure Ubuntu 22.04 LTS to prevent direct logins to the root account by using the following command:

     $ sudo passwd -l root
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** To ensure individual accountability and prevent unauthorized access, organizational users must be individually identified and authenticated.

A group authenticator is a generic account used by multiple individuals. Use of a group authenticator alone does not uniquely identify individual users. Examples of the group authenticator is the Unix OS "root" user account, the Windows "Administrator" account, the "sa" account, or a "helpdesk" account.

For example, the Unix and Windows operating systems offer a "switch user" capability allowing users to authenticate with their individual credentials and, when needed, "switch" to the administrator role. This method provides for unique individual authentication prior to using a group authenticator.

Users (and any processes acting on behalf of users) must be uniquely identified and authenticated for all accesses other than those accesses explicitly identified and documented by the organization, which outlines specific user actions that can be performed on the operating system without identification or authentication.

Requiring individuals to be authenticated with an individual authenticator prior to using a group authenticator allows for traceability of actions, as well as adding an additional level of protection of the actions that can be taken with group account knowledge.

**Threat & control context:** Well-known accounts (root, Administrator, Guest) are guaranteed to exist with predictable names, which makes them ideal targets. Blocking direct logon forces attribution through named accounts (IA-2, AC-6(2)). Removing empty-password acceptance eliminates trivial access, and unique local admin passwords (LAPS) break pass-the-hash lateral movement across a fleet. Assess the effective result across every access path: console, SSH, RDP and network logon.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078.001 Valid Accounts: Default Accounts; T1078.003 Valid Accounts: Local Accounts; T1110 Brute Force

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-004045**: Require users to be individually authenticated before granting access to the shared accounts or resources.  
  Rev 5: IA-2 (5) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-000770**: The organization requires individuals to be authenticated with an individual authenticator when a group authenticator is employed.  
  Rev 5: n/a · Rev 4: IA-2 (5) · Rev 3: IA-2 (5) (b)

| Field | Value |

| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-2, IA-8 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-2, IA-8 |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must uniquely identify interactive users.

**Why it matters:** Every person should have their own account, and accounts that nobody is using (people who left, temporary contractors, test accounts) should be turned off. Forgotten accounts are like old keys still floating around after someone moves out. You never know who might use them.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
awk -F ":" 'list[$3]++{print $1, $3}' /etc/passwd
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** On Ubuntu, inactivity is enforced with 'INACTIVE=35' in /etc/default/useradd ('useradd -D -f 35') for new accounts and 'chage -I' for existing ones. Temporary accounts get an expiry date ('chage -E'). Check /etc/passwd and /etc/group for duplicate UIDs and GIDs ('pwck', 'grpck') and that every interactive user has a valid, owned home directory.

**Operational impact:** Before you automatically disable inactive accounts, confirm that service, break-glass and seasonal-user accounts are inventoried and either exempted with documentation or monitored.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify Ubuntu 22.04 LTS contains no duplicate User IDs (UIDs) for interactive users by using the following command:

     $ awk -F ":" 'list[$3]++{print $1, $3}' /etc/passwd

If output is produced and the accounts listed are interactive user accounts, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Edit the file "/etc/passwd" and provide each interactive user account that has a duplicate UID with a unique UID.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** To ensure accountability and prevent unauthenticated access, organizational users must be identified and authenticated to prevent potential misuse and compromise of the system.

Organizational users include organizational employees or individuals the organization deems to have equivalent status of employees (e.g., contractors). Organizational users (and processes acting on behalf of users) must be uniquely identified and authenticated to all accesses, except for the following:

1. Accesses explicitly identified and documented by the organization. Organizations document specific user actions that can be performed on the information system without identification or authentication; and

2. Accesses that occur through authorized use of group authenticators without individual authentication. Organizations may require unique identification of individuals in group accounts (e.g., shared privilege accounts) or for detailed accountability of individual activity.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000104-GPOS-00051, SRG-OS-000121-GPOS-00062

**Threat & control context:** Dormant, orphaned and shared accounts are prime persistence and initial-access vectors because nobody notices their use. AC-2 (Account Management) and its enhancements (AC-2(2) temporary/emergency account removal, AC-2(3) disable inactive accounts) require automated lifecycle enforcement. IA-2 and IA-4 require unique identifiers so actions can be attributed to individuals. Assessors typically sample accounts against an authoritative roster.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1136 Create Account; T1098 Account Manipulation

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000764**: Uniquely identify and authenticate organizational users and associate that unique identification with processes acting on behalf of those users.  
  Rev 5: IA-2 · Rev 4: IA-2 · Rev 3: IA-2
- **CCI-000804**: Uniquely identify and authenticate non-organizational users or processes acting on behalf of non-organizational users.  
  Rev 5: IA-8 · Rev 4: IA-8 · Rev 3: IA-8

### V-260545 · UBTU-22-411025 · CAT II: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS must enforce 24 hours/one day as the minimum password lifetime. Passwords for new users must have a 24 hours/one day minimum password lifetime restriction.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-260545r1015007_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000075-GPOS-00043 |
| Topic | Password Age, History & Reuse |
| CCI | CCI-004066, CCI-000198 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-5 (1) (h) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-5 (1) (d) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-5 (1) (d) |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must enforce 24 hours/one day as the minimum password lifetime. Passwords for new users must have a 24 hours/one day minimum password lifetime restriction.

**Why it matters:** This makes people change passwords every so often and stops them from simply switching back to a password they used recently. If a password was quietly stolen, it eventually stops working, a bit like changing the locks periodically in case someone copied a key.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/login.defs | PASS_MIN_DAYS | 1 |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep -i pass_min_days /etc/login.defs
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo grep -si '^[[:space:]]*PASS_MIN_DAYS\b' /etc/login.defs
```

Expected: PASS_MIN_DAYS = 1

**How it works:** On Ubuntu, defaults for new accounts come from /etc/login.defs (PASS_MAX_DAYS, PASS_MIN_DAYS), while existing accounts must be updated individually with 'chage -M/-m <days> <user>' (review with 'chage -l <user>'). History is enforced by pam_pwhistory ('remember = 5' in /etc/security/pwhistory.conf or on the module line).

**Operational impact:** Changing login.defs does not retroactively update existing accounts, so remember to run chage for current users. Exclude non-interactive service accounts from expiry only through a documented exception (or use gMSAs on Windows).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify Ubuntu 22.04 LTS enforces a 24 hours/one day minimum password lifetime for new user accounts by using the following command:

     $ grep -i pass_min_days /etc/login.defs
     PASS_MIN_DAYS    1

If "PASS_MIN_DAYS" is less than "1", is commented out, or is missing, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure Ubuntu 22.04 LTS to enforce a 24 hours/one day minimum password lifetime.

Add or modify the following line in the "/etc/login.defs" file:

PASS_MIN_DAYS    1
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Enforcing a minimum password lifetime helps to prevent repeated password changes to defeat the password reuse or history enforcement requirement. If users are allowed to immediately and continually change their password, then the password could be repeatedly changed in a short period of time to defeat the organization's policy regarding password reuse.

**Threat & control context:** Maximum age bounds the useful lifetime of a compromised credential. Minimum age plus history prevent users from cycling straight back to a known password, which would defeat the history check (IA-5(1)(d)/(e)). The trend in current guidance is to prefer event-driven rotation (on suspected compromise) over periodic rotation, but the DoD baseline values remain enforceable requirements.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110.004 Brute Force: Credential Stuffing

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-004066**: For password-based authentication, enforce organization-defined composition and complexity rules.  
  Rev 5: IA-5 (1) (h) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-000198**: The information system enforces minimum password lifetime restrictions.  
  Rev 5: n/a · Rev 4: IA-5 (1) (d) · Rev 3: IA-5 (1) (d)

### V-260547 · UBTU-22-411035 · CAT II: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS must disable account identifiers (individuals, groups, roles, and devices) after 35 days of inactivity.

| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-4 e |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-4 e |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must disable account identifiers (individuals, groups, roles, and devices) after 35 days of inactivity.

**Why it matters:** Every person should have their own account, and accounts that nobody is using (people who left, temporary contractors, test accounts) should be turned off. Forgotten accounts are like old keys still floating around after someone moves out. You never know who might use them.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *DoD / DoW*: Department of Defense (renamed Department of War in recent DISA publications).

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep INACTIVE /etc/default/useradd
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** On Ubuntu, inactivity is enforced with 'INACTIVE=35' in /etc/default/useradd ('useradd -D -f 35') for new accounts and 'chage -I' for existing ones. Temporary accounts get an expiry date ('chage -E'). Check /etc/passwd and /etc/group for duplicate UIDs and GIDs ('pwck', 'grpck') and that every interactive user has a valid, owned home directory.

**Operational impact:** Before you automatically disable inactive accounts, confirm that service, break-glass and seasonal-user accounts are inventoried and either exempted with documentation or monitored.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the account identifiers (individuals, groups, roles, and devices) are disabled after 35 days of inactivity by using the following command:

Check the account inactivity value by performing the following command:

     $ grep INACTIVE /etc/default/useradd
     INACTIVE=35

If "INACTIVE" is set to "-1" or is not set to "35", is commented out, or is missing, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure Ubuntu 22.04 LTS to disable account identifiers after 35 days of inactivity after the password expiration.

Run the following command to change the configuration for adduser:

     $ sudo useradd -D -f 35

Note: DoW recommendation is 35 days, but a lower value is acceptable. The value "0" will disable the account immediately after the password expires.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Inactive identifiers pose a risk to systems and applications because attackers may exploit an inactive identifier and potentially obtain undetected access to the system. Owners of inactive accounts will not notice if unauthorized access to their user account has been obtained.

Operating systems need to track periods of inactivity and disable application identifiers after 35 days of inactivity.

**Threat & control context:** Dormant, orphaned and shared accounts are prime persistence and initial-access vectors because nobody notices their use. AC-2 (Account Management) and its enhancements (AC-2(2) temporary/emergency account removal, AC-2(3) disable inactive accounts) require automated lifecycle enforcement. IA-2 and IA-4 require unique identifiers so actions can be attributed to individuals. Assessors typically sample accounts against an authoritative roster.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1136 Create Account; T1098 Account Manipulation

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

  Rev 5: AC-2 (3) (b) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a

### V-260548 · UBTU-22-411040 · CAT II: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS must automatically expire temporary accounts within 72 hours.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-260548r1268212_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000002-GPOS-00002 |
| Topic | Password Age, History & Reuse |
| CCI | CCI-000016, CCI-001682 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-2 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-2 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-2 (2) |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must automatically expire temporary accounts within 72 hours.

**Why it matters:** This makes people change passwords every so often and stops them from simply switching back to a password they used recently. If a password was quietly stolen, it eventually stops working, a bit like changing the locks periodically in case someone copied a key.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
chage -l <temporary_account_name> | grep -E '(Password|Account) expires'
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** On Ubuntu, defaults for new accounts come from /etc/login.defs (PASS_MAX_DAYS, PASS_MIN_DAYS), while existing accounts must be updated individually with 'chage -M/-m <days> <user>' (review with 'chage -l <user>'). History is enforced by pam_pwhistory ('remember = 5' in /etc/security/pwhistory.conf or on the module line).

**Operational impact:** Changing login.defs does not retroactively update existing accounts, so remember to run chage for current users. Exclude non-interactive service accounts from expiry only through a documented exception (or use gMSAs on Windows).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify temporary accounts have been provisioned with an expiration date of 72 hours by using the following command:

     $ sudo chage -l <temporary_account_name> | grep -E '(Password|Account) expires'
     Password expires     : Apr 1, 2024
     Account expires        : Apr 1, 2024

Verify each of these accounts has an expiration date set within 72 hours.

If any temporary accounts have no expiration date set or do not expire within 72 hours, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure Ubuntu 22.04 LTS to expire temporary accounts after 72 hours by using the following command:

     $ sudo chage -E $(date -d +3days +%Y-%m-%d) <temporary_account_name>
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Temporary accounts are privileged or nonprivileged accounts established during pressing circumstances, such as new software or hardware configuration or an incident response, where the need for prompt account activation requires bypassing normal account authorization procedures. If any inactive temporary accounts are left enabled on the system and are not either manually removed or automatically expired within 72 hours, the security posture of the system will be degraded and exposed to exploitation by unauthorized users or insider threat actors.

Temporary accounts are different from emergency accounts. Emergency accounts, also known as "last resort" or "break glass" accounts, are local logon accounts enabled on the system for emergency use by authorized system administrators to manage a system when standard logon methods are failing or not available. Emergency accounts are not subject to manual removal or scheduled expiration requirements.

The automatic expiration of temporary accounts may be extended as needed by the circumstances, but it must not be extended indefinitely. A documented permanent account should be established for privileged users who need long-term maintenance accounts.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000002-GPOS-00002, SRG-OS-000123-GPOS-00064

**Threat & control context:** Maximum age bounds the useful lifetime of a compromised credential. Minimum age plus history prevent users from cycling straight back to a known password, which would defeat the history check (IA-5(1)(d)/(e)). The trend in current guidance is to prefer event-driven rotation (on suspected compromise) over periodic rotation, but the DoD baseline values remain enforceable requirements.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110.004 Brute Force: Credential Stuffing

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000016**: Automatically remove or disable temporary and emergency accounts after an organization-defined time-period for each type of account.  
  Rev 5: AC-2 (2) · Rev 4: AC-2 (2) · Rev 3: AC-2 (2)
- **CCI-001682**: Automatically remove or disable emergency accounts after an organization-defined time period for each type of account.  
  Rev 5: AC-2 (2) · Rev 4: AC-2 (2) · Rev 3: AC-2 (2)

### V-260549 · UBTU-22-411045 · CAT III: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS must automatically lock an account until the locked account is released by an administrator when three unsuccessful logon attempts have been made.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-260549r958388_rule` |
| Severity | CAT III (low) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000021-GPOS-00005 |
| Topic | Account Lockout, Session Lock & Inactivity Timeout |
| CCI | CCI-000044, CCI-002238 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-7 a, AC-7 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-7 a, AC-7 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-7 a |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must automatically lock an account until the locked account is released by an administrator when three unsuccessful logon attempts have been made.

**Why it matters:** If someone types the wrong password a few times in a row, the account is temporarily locked so they can't keep guessing. It's like a phone that freezes after several wrong passcodes, which stops a thief from trying every possible combination.

**How important is it?** Low priority (CAT III): This setting adds an extra layer of protection. A gap here on its own is less likely to cause harm, but it weakens the overall defenses.

**Key terms:**
- *PAM*: Pluggable Authentication Modules: the Linux component that checks passwords and other sign-in requirements.
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/pam.d/common-auth | auth | [default=die]  pam_faillock.so authfail |
| Config | /etc/pam.d/common-auth | auth | sufficient          pam_faillock.so authsucc |
| Config | /etc/security/faillock.conf | deny | 3 |
| Config | /etc/security/faillock.conf | fail_interval | 900 |
| Config | /etc/security/faillock.conf | unlock_time | 0 |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep faillock /etc/pam.d/common-auth
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
sudo grep -Ew 'silent|audit|deny|fail_interval|unlock_time' /etc/security/faillock.conf
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
grep -rs 'pam_faillock.so' /etc/pam.d/common-auth
```

Expected: Line present: auth [default=die]  pam_faillock.so authfail

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo grep -si '^[[:space:]]*deny\b' /etc/security/faillock.conf
```

Expected: deny = 3

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo grep -si '^[[:space:]]*fail_interval\b' /etc/security/faillock.conf
```

Expected: fail_interval = 900

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo grep -si '^[[:space:]]*unlock_time\b' /etc/security/faillock.conf
```

Expected: unlock_time = 0

**How it works:** Ubuntu 22.04/24.04 use pam_faillock, configured in /etc/security/faillock.conf (deny, fail_interval, unlock_time, audit, silent, dir) and referenced from /etc/pam.d/common-auth (preauth/authfail lines) and common-account. Older releases used pam_tally2. Inspect with 'faillock --user <name>' and reset with 'faillock --user <name> --reset'.

**Also related (Session Lock & Inactivity Timeout):** Set GNOME locking through dconf (org/gnome/desktop/screensaver lock-enabled=true, org/gnome/desktop/session idle-delay=uint32 900) with matching locks, followed by 'dconf update'. For console sessions, install 'vlock' so users can lock a terminal, and set TMOUT=900 (readonly) in /etc/profile.d/. SSH idle termination uses ClientAliveInterval/CountMax.

**Operational impact:** Service accounts with stale cached credentials (mapped drives, scheduled tasks, mobile mail clients) can trigger repeated lockouts. Identify the lockout source (Windows Event ID 4740; faillock and audit logs on Linux) before loosening the threshold.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify that Ubuntu 22.04 LTS utilizes the "pam_faillock" module by using the following command:

     $ grep faillock /etc/pam.d/common-auth

auth     [default=die]  pam_faillock.so authfail
auth     sufficient     pam_faillock.so authsucc

If the "pam_faillock.so" module is not present in the "/etc/pam.d/common-auth" file, this is a finding.

Verify the "pam_faillock" module is configured to use the following options:

     $ sudo grep -Ew 'silent|audit|deny|fail_interval|unlock_time' /etc/security/faillock.conf
     audit
     silent
     deny = 3
     fail_interval = 900
     unlock_time = 0

If "audit" is commented out, or is missing, this is a finding.

If "silent" is commented out, or is missing, this is a finding.

If "deny" is set to a value greater than "3", is commented out, or is missing, this is a finding.

If "fail_interval" is set to a value greater than "900", is commented out, or is missing, this is a finding.

If "unlock_time" is not set to "0", is commented out, or is missing, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure Ubuntu 22.04 LTS to utilize the "pam_faillock" module.

Add or modify the following lines in the "/etc/pam.d/common-auth" file, below the "auth" definition for "pam_unix.so":

auth     [default=die]  pam_faillock.so authfail
auth     sufficient          pam_faillock.so authsucc

Configure the "pam_faillock" module to use the following options.

Add or modify the following lines in the "/etc/security/faillock.conf" file:

audit
silent
deny = 3
fail_interval = 900
unlock_time = 0
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** By limiting the number of failed logon attempts, the risk of unauthorized system access via user password guessing, otherwise known as brute-forcing, is reduced. Limits are imposed by locking the account.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000021-GPOS-00005, SRG-OS-000329-GPOS-00128

**Threat & control context:** Lockout thresholds turn online password guessing from an unlimited search into a handful of attempts per window (AC-7). The trade-off is denial of service: an attacker who knows usernames can deliberately lock out accounts, which is why DoD pairs a low threshold (3) with an administrator-unlock or timed-unlock requirement. Lockout does nothing against offline cracking of stolen hashes or against password spraying that stays below the threshold, so it complements, rather than replaces, password strength and MFA.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1110.001 Brute Force: Password Guessing; T1110.003 Brute Force: Password Spraying; T1078 Valid Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT III: any vulnerability whose existence degrades measures to protect against loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000044**: Enforce the organization-defined limit of consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user during the organization-defined time period.  
  Rev 5: AC-7 a · Rev 4: AC-7 a · Rev 3: AC-7 a
- **CCI-002238**: Automatically lock the account or node for either an organization-defined time period, until the locked account or node is released by an administrator, or delays the next logon prompt according to the organization-defined delay algorithm when the maximum number of unsuccessful logon attempts is exceeded.  
  Rev 5: AC-7 b · Rev 4: AC-7 b · Rev 3: n/a

### V-260550 · UBTU-22-412010 · CAT III: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS must enforce a delay of at least four seconds between logon prompts following a failed logon attempt.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-260550r991588_rule` |
| Severity | CAT III (low) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00226 |
| Topic | Authentication Stack (PAM, SSSD, Directory) |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must enforce a delay of at least four seconds between logon prompts following a failed logon attempt.

**Why it matters:** Behind the sign-in screen is a chain of checks: the password is right, the account isn't locked, the password isn't expired, and so on. This rule makes sure every check in that chain is present and in the correct order, like making sure every guard at a multi-checkpoint entrance is at their post.

**How important is it?** Low priority (CAT III): This setting adds an extra layer of protection. A gap here on its own is less likely to cause harm, but it weakens the overall defenses.

**Key terms:**
- *PAM*: Pluggable Authentication Modules: the Linux component that checks passwords and other sign-in requirements.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/pam.d/common-auth | auth | required     pam_faildelay.so     delay=4000000 |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep pam_faildelay /etc/pam.d/common-auth
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
grep -rs 'pam_faildelay.so' /etc/pam.d/common-auth
```

Expected: Line present: auth required     pam_faildelay.so     delay=4000000

**How it works:** Ubuntu's PAM stacks are /etc/pam.d/common-auth, common-account, common-password and common-session. They are regenerated by 'pam-auth-update' from profiles in /usr/share/pam-configs/, so persistent changes belong in a custom profile there or must be re-checked after package updates. SSSD (if used) is configured in /etc/sssd/sssd.conf (mode 0600, owned by root).

**Operational impact:** PAM mistakes can lock everyone out, including root. Test changes from a second, still-open root session, and keep console access available.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify Ubuntu 22.04 LTS enforces a delay of at least four seconds between logon prompts following a failed logon attempt by using the following command:

     $ grep pam_faildelay /etc/pam.d/common-auth
     auth     required     pam_faildelay.so     delay=4000000

If "delay" is not set to "4000000" or greater, the line is commented out, or is missing, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure Ubuntu 22.04 LTS to enforce a delay of at least four seconds between logon prompts following a failed logon attempt.

Add or modify the following line in the "/etc/pam.d/common-auth" file:

auth     required     pam_faildelay.so     delay=4000000
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Limiting the number of logon attempts over a certain time interval reduces the chances that an unauthorized user may gain access to an account.

**Threat & control context:** PAM and SSSD define how every Linux authentication decision is made. Misordered or optional modules silently bypass controls such as faillock, pwquality and pwhistory. Credential caching lifetimes trade availability against revocation latency, so a revoked account keeps working offline until its cache expires. These settings support IA-2, IA-5(13) (expiration of cached authenticators), AC-7, AC-9 (previous logon notification) and AC-10 (concurrent session control).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1556.003 Modify Authentication Process: Pluggable Authentication Modules; T1110 Brute Force

**Severity rationale:** CAT III: any vulnerability whose existence degrades measures to protect against loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

Limiting the number of allowed users and sessions per user is helpful in reducing the risks related to denial-of-service (DoS) attacks.

This requirement addresses concurrent sessions for information system accounts and does not address concurrent sessions by single users via multiple system accounts. The maximum number of concurrent sessions should be defined based upon mission needs and the operational environment for each system.

**Threat & control context:** PAM and SSSD define how every Linux authentication decision is made. Misordered or optional modules silently bypass controls such as faillock, pwquality and pwhistory. Credential caching lifetimes trade availability against revocation latency, so a revoked account keeps working offline until its cache expires. These settings support IA-2, IA-5(13) (expiration of cached authenticators), AC-7, AC-9 (previous logon notification) and AC-10 (concurrent session control).

### V-260553 · UBTU-22-412025 · CAT II: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS must allow users to directly initiate a session lock for all connection types.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-260553r1015010_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000030-GPOS-00011 |
| Topic | Session Lock & Inactivity Timeout |
| CCI | CCI-000057, CCI-000060, CCI-000058 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-11 a, AC-11 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-11 a, AC-11 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-11 a, AC-11 (1) |
| Implemented via | Software package |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must allow users to directly initiate a session lock for all connection types.

**Why it matters:** If you walk away from the computer and forget to lock it, it will lock itself after a short time (15 minutes for DoD) and hide what was on the screen. Anyone who sits down then has to sign in again. It's like a car that locks its doors automatically when you walk away.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Package | apt | vlock | Installed |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
dpkg -l | grep vlock
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
dpkg -l vlock 2>/dev/null | grep '^ii' || echo 'package vlock is not installed'
```

Expected: Package must be installed.

**How it works:** Set GNOME locking through dconf (org/gnome/desktop/screensaver lock-enabled=true, org/gnome/desktop/session idle-delay=uint32 900) with matching locks, followed by 'dconf update'. For console sessions, install 'vlock' so users can lock a terminal, and set TMOUT=900 (readonly) in /etc/profile.d/. SSH idle termination uses ClientAliveInterval/CountMax.

**Operational impact:** Users running long unattended interactive jobs may be disconnected. Kiosk or operations displays that must stay visible need a documented exception and compensating physical controls.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify Ubuntu 22.04 LTS has the "vlock" package installed by using the following command:

     $ dpkg -l | grep vlock
     ii     vlock     2.2.2-10     amd64     Virtual Console locking program

If "vlock" is not installed, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Install the "vlock" package by using the following command:

     $ sudo apt-get install vlock
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** A session lock is a temporary action taken when a user stops work and moves away from the immediate physical vicinity of the information system but does not want to log out because of the temporary nature of the absence.

The session lock is implemented at the point where session activity can be determined. Rather than be forced to wait for a period of time to expire before the user session can be locked, Ubuntu 22.04 LTS need to provide users with the ability to manually invoke a session lock so users may secure their session if they need to temporarily vacate the immediate physical vicinity.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000030-GPOS-00011, SRG-OS-000031-GPOS-00012

**Threat & control context:** Unattended, unlocked sessions are an opportunistic access path for insiders and visitors, so physical access becomes logical access. AC-11 (device lock, 15 minutes in DoD), AC-11(1) (pattern-hiding displays) and AC-12 (session termination) require automatic locking that the user can't override, re-authentication to unlock, and concealment of on-screen content. Smart-card removal locking extends this to CAC workflows.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000057**: Prevent further access to the system by initiating a device lock after organization-defined time period of inactivity; and/or requiring the user to initiate a device lock before leaving the system unattended.  
  Rev 5: AC-11 a · Rev 4: AC-11 a · Rev 3: AC-11 a
- **CCI-000060**: Conceal, via the device lock, information previously visible on the display with a publicly viewable image.  
  Rev 5: AC-11 (1) · Rev 4: AC-11 (1) · Rev 3: AC-11 (1)
- **CCI-000058**: The information system provides the capability for users to directly initiate session lock mechanisms.  
  Rev 5: n/a · Rev 4: AC-11 a · Rev 3: AC-11 a

### V-260554 · UBTU-22-412030 · CAT II: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS must automatically exit interactive command shell user sessions after 15 minutes of inactivity.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-260554r958636_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000279-GPOS-00109 |
| Topic | Privilege Elevation (UAC / sudo) |
| CCI | CCI-002361 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-12 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-12 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Remediation command |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must automatically exit interactive command shell user sessions after 15 minutes of inactivity.

**Why it matters:** Even administrators work day-to-day without full power, and the system asks them to confirm, often by re-entering a password, before doing anything that could change important settings. That way, a harmful program can't quietly use admin power behind their back. It's like a bank requiring a second signature for large withdrawals.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Remediation command. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep -E "\bTMOUT=[0-9]+" /etc/bash.bashrc /etc/profile.d/*
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** On Ubuntu, sudo policy lives in /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d/ (always edit with 'visudo', validate with 'visudo -c'). STIG items include removing NOPASSWD and !authenticate, setting 'Defaults timestamp_timeout=0', and restricting 'ALL ALL=(ALL) ALL'. 'su' is restricted to the wheel group with pam_wheel in /etc/pam.d/su.

**Operational impact:** Turning off password-less sudo affects automation such as Ansible and cron jobs. Use dedicated automation accounts with tightly scoped command lists and documented exceptions. Disabling UAC (EnableLUA = 0) is not acceptable and also breaks Store/UWP apps.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify Ubuntu 22.04 LTS is configured to automatically exit interactive command shell user sessions after 15 minutes of inactivity or less by using the following command:

     $ sudo grep -E "\bTMOUT=[0-9]+" /etc/bash.bashrc /etc/profile.d/*
     /etc/profile.d/99-terminal_tmout.sh:TMOUT=900

If "TMOUT" is not set to "900" or less, is set to "0", is commented out, or missing, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure Ubuntu 22.04 LTS to exit interactive command shell user sessions after 15 minutes of inactivity.

Create and/or append a custom file under "/etc/profile.d/" by using the following command:

     $ sudo su -c "echo TMOUT=900 >> /etc/profile.d/99-terminal_tmout.sh"

This will set a timeout value of 15 minutes for all future sessions.

To set the timeout for the current sessions, execute the following command over the terminal session:

     $ export TMOUT=900
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Terminating an idle interactive command shell user session within a short time period reduces the window of opportunity for unauthorized personnel to take control of it when left unattended in a virtual terminal or physical console.

**Threat & control context:** Elevation controls make privilege use deliberate, authenticated and auditable (AC-6(1)/(2)/(9)/(10), IA-11 re-authentication). UAC's secure-desktop prompt resists UI spoofing and input injection by malware running in the user's session. sudo restrictions (no NOPASSWD, no '!authenticate', short timestamp_timeout, no blanket ALL grants) prevent silent escalation by any process running as an admin user. Every elevation event should produce an audit record.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1548.002 Abuse Elevation Control: Bypass UAC; T1548.003 Abuse Elevation Control: Sudo and Sudo Caching; T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002361**: Automatically terminate a user session after organization-defined conditions or trigger events requiring session disconnect.  
  Rev 5: AC-12 · Rev 4: AC-12 · Rev 3: n/a

### V-260555 · UBTU-22-412035 · CAT II: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS default filesystem permissions must be defined in such a way that all authenticated users can read and modify only their own files.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-260555r991590_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00228 |
| Topic | File & Directory Permissions |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Config file setting |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer's default filesystem permissions must be defined in such a way that all authenticated users can read and modify only their own files.

**Why it matters:** Every file on a computer has a label saying who owns it and who can read or change it. This rule makes sure sensitive files, such as the list of password fingerprints or system settings, can only be touched by the right people. It's like keeping personnel files in a locked HR cabinet rather than on the break-room table.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Config | /etc/login.defs | UMASK | 077 |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
grep -i '^\s*umask' /etc/login.defs
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
sudo grep -si '^[[:space:]]*UMASK\b' /etc/login.defs
```

Expected: UMASK = 077

**How it works:** Check mode and ownership with 'stat -c "%a %U %G %n" <path>' and fix them with 'chmod', 'chown' and 'chgrp'. Find unowned files with 'find / -xdev -nouser -o -nogroup'. Default permissions for new files come from UMASK in /etc/login.defs. 'dpkg --verify' highlights packaged files that have changed.

**Operational impact:** Tightening permissions can break applications that read their configuration as a non-root user. Prefer group-based access over loosening the mode, and re-check after package updates, which can reset modes.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify Ubuntu 22.04 LTS defines default permissions for all authenticated users in such a way that the user can read and modify only their own files by using the following command:

     $ grep -i '^\s*umask' /etc/login.defs
     UMASK 077

If the "UMASK" variable is set to "000", this is a finding with the severity raised to a CAT I.

If "UMASK" is not set to "077", is commented out, or is missing, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure Ubuntu 22.04 LTS to define the default permissions for all authenticated users in such a way that the user can read and modify only their own files.

Add or modify the following line in the "/etc/login.defs" file:

UMASK 077
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Setting the most restrictive default permissions ensures newly created accounts do not have unnecessary access.

**Threat & control context:** Permissive ownership or modes on credentials (shadow, SSH host keys), libraries, system binaries, cron and boot configuration, and log files allow tampering, credential theft and execution-flow hijacking. This is AC-3 / AC-6 least privilege applied at the file-system layer, plus CM-5(6) (privilege to change software libraries). Unowned files and world-writable directories without the sticky bit are common persistence and escalation footholds.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1222 File and Directory Permissions Modification; T1574 Hijack Execution Flow; T1548.001 Abuse Elevation Control: Setuid and Setgid

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

### V-288817 · UBTU-22-412040 · CAT II: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS must not assign an interactive login shell for system accounts.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-288817r1261441_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000445-GPOS-00199 |
| Topic | Account Lifecycle Management |
| CCI | CCI-002696 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SI-6 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SI-6 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Procedural / documentation |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must not assign an interactive login shell for system accounts.

**Why it matters:** Every person should have their own account, and accounts that nobody is using (people who left, temporary contractors, test accounts) should be turned off. Forgotten accounts are like old keys still floating around after someone moves out. You never know who might use them.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Procedural / documentation. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
awk -F: '(($3 > 0 && $3 < 1000) && $1 !~ /^(halt|sync|shutdown)$/ && $7 !~ /(nologin|false)$/) {print $1 ":" $3 ":" $7}' /etc/passwd
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** On Ubuntu, inactivity is enforced with 'INACTIVE=35' in /etc/default/useradd ('useradd -D -f 35') for new accounts and 'chage -I' for existing ones. Temporary accounts get an expiry date ('chage -E'). Check /etc/passwd and /etc/group for duplicate UIDs and GIDs ('pwck', 'grpck') and that every interactive user has a valid, owned home directory.

**Operational impact:** Before you automatically disable inactive accounts, confirm that service, break-glass and seasonal-user accounts are inventoried and either exempted with documentation or monitored.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify Ubuntu 22.04 LTS system accounts do not have an interactive login shell with the following command:

Run the following command to list any system account (UID < 1000) that has an interactive shell, excluding authorized system utility accounts (root, sync, shutdown, halt):

$ awk -F: '(($3 > 0 && $3 < 1000) && $1 !~ /^(halt|sync|shutdown)$/ && $7 !~ /(nologin|false)$/) {print $1 ":" $3 ":" $7}' /etc/passwd

If the command returns any output, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure Ubuntu 22.04 LTS so that all noninteractive accounts on the system do not have an interactive shell assigned to them.

If the system account needs a shell assigned for mission operations, document the need with the information system security officer (ISSO).

Run the following command to disable the interactive shell for a specific noninteractive user account:

$ sudo usermod -s /usr/sbin/nologin <user>
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Ensuring shells are not given to system accounts upon login makes it more difficult for attackers to use system accounts.

**Threat & control context:** Dormant, orphaned and shared accounts are prime persistence and initial-access vectors because nobody notices their use. AC-2 (Account Management) and its enhancements (AC-2(2) temporary/emergency account removal, AC-2(3) disable inactive accounts) require automated lifecycle enforcement. IA-2 and IA-4 require unique identifiers so actions can be attributed to individuals. Assessors typically sample accounts against an authoritative roster.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1136 Create Account; T1098 Account Manipulation

### V-260556 · UBTU-22-431010 · CAT II: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS must have the "apparmor" package installed.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-260556r958702_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000312-GPOS-00124 |
| Topic | Least Functionality: Remove Unneeded Software |
| CCI | CCI-001764, CCI-001774, CCI-002165 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 (2), CM-7 (5) (b), AC-3 (4) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 (2), CM-7 (5) (b), AC-3 (4) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Software package |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must have the "apparmor" package installed.

**Why it matters:** Every program on a computer is another possible way in for an attacker. This rule removes software the system doesn't need, especially old programs known to be unsafe. It's like clearing clutter out of a house: fewer things lying around means fewer things that can be broken or misused.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Package | apt | apparmor | Installed |

**Command-line validation:**

*Bash* (from DISA check text)

```text
dpkg -l | grep apparmor
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*Bash* (generated from the setting)

```text
dpkg -l apparmor 2>/dev/null | grep '^ii' || echo 'package apparmor is not installed'
```

Expected: Package must be installed.

**How it works:** Remove packages with 'apt-get remove --purge <pkg>' (purge also deletes their configuration files) and verify with 'dpkg -l | grep <pkg>'. Check what else 'apt' plans to remove before confirming the transaction.

**Operational impact:** Check that no application depends on the component before removing it (e.g. legacy scripts using PowerShell 2.0, tools that shell out to telnet or ftp). Keep a record of what was removed so it can be restored if a mission requirement is identified.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify Ubuntu 22.04 LTS has the "apparmor" package installed by using the following command:

     $ dpkg -l | grep apparmor
     ii     apparmor     3.0.4-2ubuntu2.3     amd64     user-space parser utility for AppArmor

If the "apparmor" package is not installed, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Install the "appArmor" package by using the following command:

     $ sudo apt-get install apparmor
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Control of program execution is a mechanism used to prevent execution of unauthorized programs. Some operating systems may provide a capability that runs counter to the mission or provides users with functionality that exceeds mission requirements. This includes functions and services installed at the operating system level.

Some of the programs, installed by default, may be harmful or may not be necessary to support essential organizational operations (e.g., key missions, functions). Removal of executable programs is not always possible; therefore, establishing a method of preventing program execution is critical to maintaining a secure system baseline.

Methods for complying with this requirement include restricting execution of programs in certain environments, while preventing execution in other environments; or limiting execution of certain program functionality based on organization-defined criteria (e.g., privileges, subnets, sandboxed environments, or roles).

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000312-GPOS-00124, SRG-OS-000368-GPOS-00154, SRG-OS-000370-GPOS-00155

**Threat & control context:** Every installed package, role and feature is potential attack surface, and some (telnet, rsh, TFTP, SMBv1, PowerShell 2.0) are inherently insecure or allow security controls to be bypassed. For example, PowerShell 2.0 bypasses script-block logging and AMSI. CM-7 (least functionality) and CM-7(1)/(2) require removing what isn't mission-necessary. Removal also reduces patch burden and false positives in vulnerability scans.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application; T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services; T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

  Rev 5: CM-7 (2) · Rev 4: CM-7 (2) · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-001774**: Employ a deny-all, permit-by-exception policy to allow the execution of authorized software programs on the system.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 (5) (b) · Rev 4: CM-7 (5) (b) · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-002165**: Enforce organization-defined discretionary access control policies over defined subjects and objects.
